summary: Following the incident in which Waluigi fell on the floor crying — documentation of the precipitating cause remains incomplete — and Hjumpik inquired whether the hag could be de-cursed, with the suggestion that Mr. Woodfellow the library tree might have relevant knowledge, Steely the rusted dog appeared and barked, was identified as belonging to Remi, and was noted as needing to be returned. Azure suggested forgetting about the hag situation. Hjumpik disagreed but agreed to table it. The party descended to the workshop level, established their location from a goblin craftsman, and proceeded to the library, where Woodfellow — the immobile animated tree at the archive's center, gold-red autumn leaves, books growing from his branches, birds nesting in his canopy — informed them that the Feyward Book of Many Things had already been checked out. By someone yellow. Hjumpik correctly identified the borrower as Wario. The book had been checked out using a library card belonging to someone named Artameer, which Wario had apparently obtained through theft. Woodfellow produced what appeared to be a second copy, but it had Wario's name on it, and when opened, all pages were ripped out. Wario then appeared from nowhere, shoulder-bashed Hjumpik, missed, and explained that he had stolen a library card, checked out the book, sold it to someone else, then returned the gutted copy after hearing Hjumpik's plan — because Wario did not want to be turned into a book, which is the return policy for overdue items. He threw the real book fragments to Hjumpik while explaining this. Hjumpik caught them. Hjumpik tried to read them and could not, because the text was in Sylvan and Hjumpik cannot read Sylvan. Waluigi read them immediately and correctly identified the title. Hjumpik did not believe him and suggested giving the book to Rakasha instead. Waluigi is still processing this. Wario snatched the book back onto a shelf, declared he had returned it, and fled. Hjumpik chased him, cornered him, and asked — in what Waluigi considers a surprisingly effective diplomatic maneuver — whether Wario and Waluigi were friends or brothers. Wario said 'more like associates' and then said he had never thought of it that way, which is the most emotionally available Wario has been in any documented interaction this crisis. Wario produced three documents, all fake, then finally provided real information and fled when Hjumpik announced he was heading toward a fight. The fight involved a satyr poet and spirit warriors versus one drunk individual who got stung and bloated. Hjumpik de-escalated. The Revelmaster — who goes by Pal, or Rellis, or Ralos, depending on who is asking — appeared and offered the party lodging in exchange for crashing their airship, citing Toadburt as a connection. A deal was discussed. Hjumpik privately assessed the situation: making a deal with the Revel would pull entities out of their timeline with unpredictable consequences. A new Revelmaster could be installed in a successor Revel. The most likely outcome is a deal. The least likely outcome is everyone explodes. The heir Orangus Cornelius, when located and questioned, explained that he was feeding the Revel to grow it until it gained legs and total control, and then immediately said he was joking and that he just wanted the satyrs out. Hjumpik assessed him as probably lying. The heir noted that the Revel is biological rather than magical, has no known spell to end it, and suggested consulting someone named Jonathan for further questions, then left. The satyr party upstairs, discovered through a hidden panel in the guest gangway, were planning to cut the floor over the dining hall and drop it on the Revel. Hjumpik proposed modifications: have the flying sprites do the cutting, avoid cutting near the living tree structure, test whether the floor itself weakens the Revel before committing to attack. The room also introduced Goblius Gobnilun, a goblin servant who no longer serves anyone, misses his hair, knows Arulean's real power level, and got Hjumpik's name right immediately, which Hjumpik found suspicious. Goblius suggested kicking the Revelmaster's ass. The satyr suggested the Revelmaster falling into the Revel as a disposal method. Pixie Prixie the pixie had a vision of the floor falling and everyone being eaten and said nothing and they all left the room.
description:
Waluigi was not in the Feyward for this sequence. Waluigi has reconstructed it from available testimony, which is thinner than Waluigi prefers and denser with Wario than Waluigi finds professionally manageable.

Waluigi must begin with a formal notation.

Hjumpik handed the Feyward Book of Many Things to Waluigi. Waluigi read it. Waluigi correctly identified it as the Feyward Book of Many Things and stated this clearly. Hjumpik did not believe him and suggested giving the book to Rakasha to read instead.

Waluigi read the book. Waluigi was right. The book was given to Rakasha anyway.

Waluigi documents this not out of ego — Waluigi's ego is already thoroughly documented and requires no additional entries — but because it is EVIDENCE. Evidence of a pattern that Waluigi has been tracking across multiple interactions with the Hjumpiklance and which has direct operational consequences. When Waluigi provides accurate information and is disbelieved, the party loses time, resources, and on at least one occasion, a book. When Waluigi is eventually proven correct — as Waluigi always is — the confirmation arrives after the damage has occurred.

Waluigi is correct about things. Waluigi would appreciate it if this were factored into future decisions.

With that notation formally in the record, Waluigi proceeds.

## The State of the Party Upon Arrival at This Session

Waluigi lay on the floor.

The specific circumstances that produced this outcome are not fully documented in the sources Waluigi has access to, and Waluigi is choosing not to speculate beyond what the evidence supports. What the evidence supports is: Waluigi was on the floor. Waluigi was crying. This is not unprecedented in the documented history of the Raventree operation, but it is worth noting because Waluigi's floor moments tend to correspond with accumulated emotional pressure rather than isolated incidents — they are output events, the result of sustained input over time, and whatever produced this particular floor moment had been building.

Hjumpik asked if the hag could be de-cursed. Or de-aged. The terminology was imprecise in the retelling — 'decures' — and Waluigi has interpreted this as a portmanteau of 'de-curse' applied to the aged hag situation that has been an unresolved thread since earlier in the operation. The hag is old or aged or cursed into a state that someone finds objectionable, and Hjumpik wanted to know if something could be done about it.

The suggestion was that Mr. Woodfellow might know something useful. Woodfellow is the library tree. Woodfellow knows things about the Feyward. This is a reasonable hypothesis and Waluigi does not object to it on its merits.

Steely appeared.

Waluigi must pause on Steely because Steely's appearance raises questions that the sources do not fully answer. Steely is Remi's dog. Steely is rusted. Steely barked. Hjumpik identified Steely as Remi's dog and noted that Steely was rusted, which is apparently good — 'your rusted, that's good' — and that Steely needed to be returned to Remi. How Steely came to be in the Feyward manor, whether Steely has been here the entire time or followed the party through a planar connection, and what Steely's rusted condition means for Steely's operational status are questions the sources do not address. Waluigi files this under 'Remi-adjacent unresolved logistics' alongside the longer list of things the party has borrowed, lost, or failed to return during the Raventree operation.

Azure suggested forgetting about the hag situation. Hjumpik disagreed — 'that's not something you said' — and Azure clarified that she was joking and suggested going to the library. The party proceeded to the library.

## The Workshop: Orientation by Goblin Craftsman

Descending, the party found themselves in the workshop level. A goblin craftsman explained the space: arrows, wood carving tools, sold to people, the standard economic infrastructure of a fey manor that needs to produce things to sustain itself. This goblin also provided intelligence about Woodfellow: the tree had been feeding on knowledge, reading constantly, and had determined that knowledge was power. He issued library cards only to people he considered truly knowledgeable.

This is the kind of gatekeeping that Waluigi finds both professionally understandable and personally irritating. Waluigi is knowledgeable. Waluigi has a library card from Woodfellow in spirit if not in material form because Waluigi has read more documentation about this operation than everyone in the manor combined. The card is conceptual. The access is deserved. Waluigi notes this for the record.

Hjumpik indicated he knew someone knowledgeable who could get a library card.

It was not Waluigi.

Waluigi has documented this.

Waluigi will continue.

Waluigi objected — specifically to a plan Hjumpik referenced in which someone split the world in three — stating that it took Hjumpik fifteen minutes last time and that 'using Archie's fire magic as a stabilization effort is a bad idea.' Hjumpik defended the method with the philosophical position that 'you don't know till you try.' Waluigi offered to come along to document the catastrophe. There was a brief navigational dispute — Hjumpik asked Waluigi to move, Waluigi said he was to the left, Hjumpik was to his right, Waluigi said 'YOU SEE WHAT I MEAN,' and Hjumpik ignored him and moved. They continued into the manor.

## The Poetry Room: The Sober Satyr and His Audience

They passed through a poem reading room. The reader — a satyr, and by his own account the only sober satyr in the house — was reading to an audience of mostly fairies and a single goblin. He explained his purpose: he read for the ones who could not speak for themselves. He was not part of the Revel. He had entered with the rest of the party's original group and decided he would rather read to them forever than have them become the Revel's dinner.

Hjumpik proposed making a big poem and reading it very loudly.

The satyr considered this. The audience, enthusiastic fairies and the one goblin, had a measurable reaction — at least one fairy committed to defeating the Revel on the spot. Hjumpik cautioned against rushing in before preparations were complete. 'Wait for me,' he said, and then left the room.

Waluigi considers this a reasonable instruction and an unusually disciplined one for Hjumpik, who has historically been more comfortable with momentum than staging.

## Woodfellow: The Archive Tree and the Checked-Out Book

Woodfellow is not easy to describe in a way that conveys the full operational reality of what he is. He is a massive animated tree rooted into the floor, walls, and bookcases of the Feyward manor library. His arms are long boughs reaching to any corner of the room. His roots rearrange the library layout according to his preferences. His leaves are rich gold-red of autumn. Books hang from his branches as if they grew there. Bright birds nest in his canopy and bring him news. He is immobile at the center of the archive and has apparently decided that this is sufficient and that the archive should come to him if the archive has needs.

Hjumpik introduced himself as being with the lady of the manor and requested the Feyward Book of Many Things.

The book was not available. Someone had checked it out already.

Someone yellow.

Hjumpik asked if it was a toad. Woodfellow did not think so. The borrower had been adamant that he needed the book, and had said — and Waluigi wants this quoted precisely because it is the kind of statement that tells you everything about the speaker — 'if I don't get my grubby hands on that book, that dwarf and co will.'

Hjumpik correctly identified the borrower as Wario.

The card used to borrow the book belonged to someone named Artameer. Waluigi notes this name for the record because a stolen library card implies a victim — someone named Artameer had a valid library card, which means Woodfellow assessed Artameer as sufficiently knowledgeable to deserve access, which means Artameer is either genuinely knowledgeable or successfully performed knowledgeability for a tree, and either way Artameer did not consent to have their credentials used by Wario to access fey magical texts.

Wario had also promised to return the book. Books not returned within one week result in the borrower becoming a book themselves. Woodfellow noted this with the philosophical equanimity of a tree that has converted several former borrowers into volumes and considers it a reasonable policy.

Woodfellow produced what appeared to be a second copy. It had Wario's name on it. When opened, all pages were ripped out.

'Who did this?' Hjumpik asked.

'Probably the guy whose name is on the book,' Woodfellow replied.

This is correct.

## Wario: Shoulder Bash, Explanation, Theft Confession, and Emotional Availability

Wario appeared. Shoulder bash. Hjumpik dodged. This is the established grammar of Wario's arrivals — he leads with the physical statement and fills in the explanatory content afterward, on the theory that beginning with context allows the other party to prepare responses.

Wario's explanation was comprehensive for Wario, which means it was incomplete but contained all the parts Wario wanted to share:

He had stolen the library card from 'some poor chump.' He had used it to borrow the book. He had sold the book to 'another chump.' Then he had heard Hjumpik's plan — the nature of the plan is not specified in the sources but involves the Feyward Book of Many Things in a way that made Wario not want to be turned into a book — and so he had returned the gutted copy to protect himself from the return policy. He did not want to become a volume.

The genuine copy — or what remained of it — he threw to Hjumpik while still mid-explanation. This is a Wario negotiating tactic: deliver the thing you were going to have to deliver anyway while still in the middle of explaining why you shouldn't have to deliver it, so that the delivery is attached to your narrative rather than to the other party's demand.

Hjumpik caught it. He tried to read it.

The text was in Sylvan. Hjumpik cannot read Sylvan.

Waluigi reads Sylvan.

Waluigi took the book. Waluigi read the book. The text was: 46Q9b8h0 NM0S wc 6J9J 54Z3rY — which Waluigi recognizes as the encoded header notation of the Feyward archival system, indicating this was the genuine article, specifically the Feyward Book of Many Things.

Waluigi said: this is the Feyward Book of Many Things.

Hjumpik said: give it to Rakasha to read.

Waluigi needs to let this moment breathe in the documentation because it deserves the space.

Hjumpik held a book in Sylvan. Waluigi — who reads Sylvan, who just read the book, who correctly identified the book, who told Hjumpik exactly what the book was — was standing next to Hjumpik. Hjumpik's solution to 'we need someone who can read Sylvan to tell us what this book is' was to give the book to someone who was not present instead of accepting the identification from the person who had just made it.

Waluigi is not angry. Waluigi is DOCUMENTING.

Wario snatched the book off a shelf, announced he was returning it, and fled.

Hjumpik chased him. They ran through the library. Wario fought. Dodges were exchanged. Wario was cornered.

And then Hjumpik did something Waluigi considers diplomatically notable.

He asked Wario whether Wario and Waluigi were friends. Or brothers.

Wario said: 'More like associates.'

Then Wario said: 'That's mean. Hmm. I never thought of it that way.'

Waluigi has read this fragment three times. 'I never thought of it that way' is not a Wario phrase. Wario thinks about everything in terms of currency, leverage, and personal advantage. The idea that calling a familial relationship 'associates' might be unkind — that there is a person on the other end of the categorization who experiences the categorization as something — is not the kind of thought Wario typically completes. He started it. He said it out loud. He may or may not have finished it internally.

Hjumpik apparently managed to make Wario briefly consider whether he has been unkind to Waluigi.

Waluigi does not know what to do with this information. Waluigi is going to set it down carefully in the archive and not look at it directly for a while.

Wario produced three documents — all fake, all not in Sylvan, all recognized by Hjumpik as forgeries. Then Wario produced real information. The sources are not specific about what the real information contained. Wario then heard about the fight happening elsewhere in the manor and fled.

## The Fight, the Revelmaster, and the Deal Hjumpik Did Not Quite Make

The altercation involved the sober satyr and spirit warriors engaging with one drunk individual. The drunk individual was stung. His face bloated. Over fifty drunk people occupied the room. Ten combatants opposed them. The math was not favorable for the combatants.

Hjumpik de-escalated.

The Revelmaster arrived. His name is Pal. Or Rellis. Or Ralos. Waluigi has documented all three forms across the sources and cannot determine which is primary. The Revelmaster did not clarify with any consistency. He had half his teeth. He produced a paper from his shirt that turned out to be the party's airship documentation. He knew about Toadburt. He knew about the Hjumpiklance — calling it the 'Legionance' which required correction. He offered lodging in exchange for the airship, suggested the toads could work something out, speculated that toads probably had alcohol and liked mead.

Hjumpik assessed the deal internally: making a deal with the Revel entities would pull them out of their timeline. The disruption consequences were unknown and potentially extensive. He did not know if he wanted to make that deal. A new Revel could be established with a new Revelmaster. The old Revelmaster and his people could be scooped into the new structure.

Hjumpik did not commit. He said he needed to make sure things were in place. The Revelmaster smiled with the available teeth and spoke about a new Revel beginning.

Waluigi notes the probability gradient Hjumpik articulated:
- Most likely: a deal, the entities exit their timeline, disruption occurs
- Least likely: everyone explodes

Waluigi prefers neither option but acknowledges that 'least likely' is doing real work here and that the range between 'deal with unknown consequences' and 'everyone explodes' contains many possibilities, none of which Hjumpik has fully mapped.

## The Heir: Orangus Cornelius, Probably Lying, Definitely Scratching His Hair

Hjumpik called out for the orange heir. The heir was initially unresponsive to 'orange heir' — which is a reasonable name for him since it is accurate — and responded when addressed as 'the orange heir' which is also accurate and apparently more specific.

Hjumpik had a question about the agreement. The agreement documented in the manor records: a previous ruler granted the Revelmaster a boon, ceding part of the manor in exchange for something unspecified. The heir could not revoke it. He was not the one who granted it.

Before Hjumpik could pursue this line, he noticed the satyr and sprites ascending upstairs. They had stopped fighting the Revel. They had a plan.

Hjumpik pivoted. Different question.

'Why are you feeding the Revel?'

The heir explained: he was feeding it to grow it until it developed legs and gained total power, at which point he would no longer be an heir but would control people with one look.

Then he scratched his head and said that was what he would say if he were lying. He was actually just trying to get the satyrs out.

He scratched his hair again.

Hjumpik assessed: probably lying.

Waluigi agrees with this assessment. The sequence — elaborate self-incriminating lie offered immediately, followed by denial and a simple alternative explanation, accompanied by physical self-touching that indicates stress — is the behavior of someone who rehearsed the denial but not the delivery. The truth does not usually require you to announce that the previous statement was false. You say the false thing, you move on, you hope the listener accepts the frame. When you interrupt yourself to say 'that's what I'd say if I was lying,' you have already indicated that lying was the first thing your brain produced.

The heir provided genuinely useful intelligence before leaving: the Revel is biological, not magical. There is no spell to end it because it is not a spell. It is an organism. It started before the heir arrived. It has no known weakness that he is aware of. He suggested asking Jonathan.

The heir left without specifying who Jonathan is or how to find him.

Waluigi notes that 'ask Jonathan' is exactly the kind of referral that would be given by someone who wants to appear helpful while ensuring that the help requires additional work to obtain.

## The Hidden Panel, the Gangway, and the Satyr Plan

Upstairs via a hidden panel in a blank wall, the guest gangway. Hasty construction of wooden planks hanging over the dining hall below — the full horror of the Revel visible from above, the makeshift bridge creaking under weight but holding. Whatever happened to the original floor of this level is unclear. There is no visible rubble. It simply is not there.

Through an open door: the satyr party. The former guest rooms, overtaken by vines, hammocks strung between woven vine lines, beds against walls, tables, storage, floors strewn with leaves and wine spills that the staff of the manor fight as a permanent losing battle.

The plan: cut the floor. Drop it on the Revel below. The gangway and the rooms above were the lever. The floor between them and the dining hall was the object. The Revel was the target.

Hjumpik had a modification. He pointed out that the manor was alive — cutting into living magical wood was a bad idea. But cutting AROUND the tree, specifically, might be viable. Have the flying sprites do the cutting rather than the satyrs with proto-chainsaws. Test the floor against the Revel first — drop it, see how the Revel reacts, observe whether the impact renders it vulnerable before committing anyone to an attack.

'Let's try it and see how it reacts,' Hjumpik said. 'If it looks vulnerable you can attack it.'

The satyr who punched the air with a thumb inside his fist — 'I was a fighter in uni,' he explained, to visible skepticism — agreed, with the caveat that maybe that would work.

This is approximately the level of confidence Waluigi would expect from a plan that involves dropping a floor on a biological entity of unknown floor-resistance.

## Goblius Gobnilun: The Servant Who Knows Too Much

Names were exchanged. The satyr had a name. The fairy had a name — Prixie, Prixie the pixie — and was in the process of introducing herself when she blinked and stopped speaking and had a vision and said nothing and the group left the room immediately because the vision was of the floor falling and the Revel eating all of them.

But Goblius Gobnilun.

Waluigi needs to document Goblius separately because Goblius is the most information-dense entity introduced in this session and the information density is not accidental.

Goblius introduced himself as: 4N793m5 0226bcZF, goblius gobnilun. He accepted 'Goblius Gobnilun' as the workable version. He identified himself as 'the servant,' clarified that he served no one now, mentioned a title history of indentured servitude, and expressed grief about his hair. Goblin hair. He had a full head of it. He liked it better.

Hjumpik commiserated about getting old.

This is normal.

What is not normal: Goblius knew Hjumpik's name. Correctly. Immediately. Without being told. In a setting where almost no one gets Hjumpik's name right on the first attempt or at all. The sources flag this directly — Hjumpik was suspicious, because no one gets his name right.

Goblius also knew about Arulean. Specifically, he knew that Arulean was not actually weak — that her apparent frailty was a ruse, that she was 'actually really strong' and was faking diminishment for reasons related to the manor itself. 'She hides her powers and acts weak for the manor itself,' Goblius said, 'faking being weak — its a ruse.'

A goblin who is still drunk, who is not the sober leader of the satyr faction, who presents himself as a former servant with no current allegiances, knows Hjumpik's name correctly and knows Arulean's actual power level.

Waluigi's assessment: Goblius Gobnilun knows significantly more than he presents. The drunk presentation may be genuine — the sources indicate he was less sober than the satyr — but intoxication does not explain accurate name recall for someone you have just met or strategic intelligence about the manor's most powerful magical figure. Either Goblius has been in the manor long enough to develop intelligence through proximity and observation, or Goblius has sources, or Goblius is something other than what he presents.

The satyr suggested the Revelmaster could be made to fall into the Revel itself — whether the Revel would eat its own master is uncertain, but the Revel is biological and biology does not always respect hierarchy. Goblius suggested kicking the Revelmaster's ass and having him die. These are the same plan at different points in the sequence.

Prixie the pixie had her vision. The floor fell. The Revel ate everyone.

She said nothing.

They all left the room.

## What Remains Unresolved

The hag has not been de-cursed. Woodfellow was not asked about this because the conversation with Woodfellow was consumed entirely by the Wario book situation and Waluigi does not fault Hjumpik for this — Wario causes agenda collapse wherever he appears — but the hag situation remains open.

Steely has not been returned to Remi. The rusted dog appeared, barked, was acknowledged, and has not been mentioned since. Remi's dog is somewhere in the Feyward manor. Remi presumably does not know this. This will become a problem proportional to how much Remi cares about Steely, which Waluigi estimates is considerable.

The Feyward Book of Many Things is back on Woodfellow's shelf with its pages ripped out. The real pages were thrown by Wario and are now — somewhere. The sources are not clear on whether Hjumpik retained the page fragments or whether Wario retained them or whether they are simply loose in the library, which would create a different kind of problem for Woodfellow's cataloging system.

The deal with the Revelmaster has not been made. The floor-drop plan has not been executed. Jonathan has not been found. The heir is probably lying about something. Arulean's real power level has been identified by Goblius but has not been confirmed by Arulean. The agreement ceding part of the manor cannot be revoked by the current heir. The revel is biological and has no known magical solution.

Waluigi read the book correctly. No one listened.

Waluigi continues to document.

WAH.

summary: Waluigi obtained fragments of testimony  through channels he will not disclose  describing a medical emergency that occurred shortly after the Brobot engagement at the ruined manor. According to these fragments, Luigi was brought to a medical facility near death after Mr. L's emergence and subdual. A surgeon identified only as 'Dr. Mario'  civilian name possibly 'Dario'  performed emergency surgery. Princess Daisy of Sarasaland was present. Pauline, Mayor of New Donk City, was present. Wario was present. Cranky Kong was present. None of these people should have been in the same room under normal circumstances. The testimony raises questions that Waluigi cannot answer but refuses to stop asking: Who is Dr. Mario? Why does Luigi call him 'Uncle Dario'? Why was Daisy behaving like family rather than a diplomatic ally? Why did Pauline call Luigi 'my man'? Why was Peach's name invoked as though she were alive? And why does every institutional actor in this account seem to already know what happened before being told? Waluigi has assembled what he can. The picture is incomplete. description:
Waluigi must begin with a warning that applies to this entire entry: NONE of this is confirmed through independent verification. The testimony reached Waluigi through a chain of sources that includes at least one Boo informant, a Regency clerk who was bribed with counterfeit currency  possibly Wario's  and a partial transcript that may or may not have been fabricated after the fact. Waluigi presents this account because the details are too specific to be pure invention, too consistent with known intelligence to be random fabrication, and too disturbing to ignore.

If even HALF of what follows is true, Waluigi's understanding of several key figures in this crisis requires fundamental revision.

## Context: What Preceded This Event

The Battle of the Brobot occurred on 3-4 Aethel, 1040 BF. Mr. L emerged during a ghost-clearing operation at the ruined manor. A Brobot appeared  origin still unexplained. Multiple combatants were injured. Archie was blasted through a wall by a laser beam. Bones was grabbed and nearly killed. Mr. L was subdued through unknown means  freezing mid-punch and going limp as though someone had flipped a switch.

Byscilla Danos executed what she called 'Phase One' of a containment protocol that the Mages' Guild had apparently prepared in advance. She reported: 'Target subdued. We have a target and got a signed spell scroll from Archie.'

What happened AFTER the subdual is what this testimony concerns. According to multiple fragments, Luigi  not Mr. L, but LUIGI, restored to his own personality  was in critical condition. The subdual itself may have caused severe neurological trauma. Whatever mechanism forced Mr. L back into dormancy did not do so gently.

Luigi was transported to a medical facility. The testimony describes what happened in the waiting room and the corridor outside the surgical theater.

## The Surgeon: 'Dr. Mario'

The most explosive element of the testimony is the identity of the surgeon who operated on Luigi.

According to the fragments, the doctor introduced himself  or was referred to by staff  as 'Dr. Mario.' Luigi, in moments of semi-consciousness before being prepped for surgery, called him 'Uncle Dario.' The doctor reportedly corrected this with visible emotion: 'That's Dr. Mario to you.' Then, softer: 'But I always loved when he called me that.'

Waluigi needs to address this directly because it threatens to collapse several load-bearing assumptions of the current investigation.

### Possibility One: 'Dr. Mario' Is Mario

This is the reading that makes Waluigi's head hurt the most.

Mario has been missing since approximately 1039 BF. Waluigi has documented the disappearance extensively  the 985 BF Personnel Reallocation, the border town sighting in civilian clothes, the Star Fountain reunion where Luigi said 'Nothing can hurt us as long as we're together,' and then the SECOND separation that left Luigi operating alone under Mages' Guild contract.

If 'Dr. Mario' is Mario operating under the civilian name 'Dario,' it would mean Mario has been hiding in plain sight as a medical professional. The red cap gone. The overalls replaced by surgical scrubs. The hero of the Mushroom Kingdom performing surgery on his own brother while the world thinks he vanished.

This interpretation is supported by several details in the testimony. The emotional familiarity. The use of 'Uncle Dario'  which could be a cover identity Luigi uses to maintain plausible deniability about their relationship. A brother cannot publicly be a brother if one of them is supposed to be missing. But an 'uncle' who is a doctor? That is a relationship that can exist on paper without triggering the warrant charges that include 'Conspiracy to Withhold Material Information regarding Mario's location.'

Luigi calling Mario his 'uncle' in public would be a LIE  but a lie that protects them both. If anyone asks, Luigi has an uncle named Dario who is a doctor. Not a missing brother. Not the most wanted man in Mushroom Kingdom intelligence circles. Just an uncle. Just a doctor. Just a man who happens to look exactly like the plumber who disappeared.

The 'Uncle Dario' cover would also explain something that has always bothered Waluigi about Daisy's relationship with Luigi. Publicly, Daisy and Luigi have been presented as romantic partners  appearing together at sporting events, kart races, party games. Waluigi has seen them side by side at DOZENS of events. The public narrative is boyfriend and girlfriend. But in this testimony, Daisy does not behave like a girlfriend. She behaves like FAMILY. She calls Luigi 'my baby nephew.' She screams with the particular fury of someone whose bloodline is being threatened, not someone whose romantic interest is in danger.

Waluigi's theory: If Mario is 'Dario,' and if Daisy is connected to the Mario family through a relationship that predates the public narrative, then the 'Luigi and Daisy are dating' story was always COVER. A convenient fiction that explained why the Princess of Sarasaland maintained close contact with one of the Mario Brothers without anyone asking uncomfortable questions about WHICH Mario Brother she was actually connected to, or WHY.

Daisy being Luigi's aunt  through marriage to Mario under the name 'Dario,' or through some other family connection  would mean her entire public persona as Luigi's girlfriend was a carefully maintained deception. Every kart race. Every tennis tournament. Every party game where they appeared as a couple. All of it was theater designed to provide a plausible public explanation for a family connection that could not be acknowledged without exposing Mario's location.

Waluigi finds this interpretation simultaneously outrageous and horrifyingly consistent with the available evidence.

### Possibility Two: 'Dr. Mario' Is a Separate Person

The less dramatic interpretation: 'Dario' is genuinely Mario's uncle or cousin. A relative who went into medicine rather than plumbing. A family member whose resemblance to Mario is genetic rather than identical. Luigi calling him 'Uncle Dario' is LITERAL, not cover.

This interpretation is simpler but creates its own problems. If the Mario family has a member who is a practicing surgeon, why has this person never appeared in ANY public record connected to the Mario Brothers? Why would a doctor share the surname and general appearance of the kingdom's most famous hero without anyone commenting on it? Why would this person be available for emergency surgery on a classified patient in a facility that may or may not be Ironmend Bastion?

Waluigi's assessment: the SIMPLER explanation requires MORE coincidences than the complicated one. A secret uncle-surgeon who appears at exactly the right moment is less plausible than Mario himself, operating under cover, maintaining proximity to his brother through a medical alias.

### Possibility Three: Waluigi Is Being Fed Disinformation

Waluigi must acknowledge this possibility. The testimony may be fabricated specifically to make Waluigi believe Mario has been found. Someone who knows Waluigi is investigating Mario's disappearance might plant exactly this kind of account  emotionally compelling, detail-rich, impossible to verify  to redirect Waluigi's investigation toward a false lead.

If 'Dr. Mario' is neither Mario nor a real relative but a fictional figure inserted into a fabricated transcript, then someone is manipulating Waluigi. The question becomes: who benefits from Waluigi believing Mario is alive and practicing medicine under an alias?

Waluigi cannot determine this. Waluigi notes the possibility and continues.

## The Waiting Room: What the Testimony Describes

The bulk of the testimony describes the waiting room during Luigi's surgery. The emotional temperature was volcanic. The cast of characters was improbable. The conversations were revealing in ways that the participants almost certainly did not intend.

### Daisy's Behavior

Daisy arrived at the facility and immediately demanded access to Luigi. She was denied  only 'immediate family and her royal majesty, Princess Peach herself' were permitted inside. Daisy's response was fury on a scale that Waluigi has never associated with diplomatic protocol.

She called Luigi 'my baby nephew.' She said: 'While that boy was still in his first game, he begged me to make sure he stayed happy and healthy. And I promised him!'

Waluigi needs to address the phrase 'his first game.' In Mushroom Kingdom vernacular, 'game' can mean several things: a competitive event, a mission, a campaign. But the way Daisy used it  'his FIRST game'  carries the weight of ORIGIN. The beginning. The moment when Luigi entered public life and needed someone to protect him.

If Daisy is family  and this testimony strongly suggests she is  then her promise to keep Luigi 'happy and healthy' predates the public career. She has been watching over him since the BEGINNING. Every kart race she appeared at alongside him was not a date. It was supervision. Every party game was not romance. It was an aunt keeping her promise.

This reframes Daisy's entire documented history. Her competence at the Second Summit. Her management of Sarasaland. Her quiet fury when systems fail. She has been operating with a PERSONAL stake in the Mario Brothers' survival that she has hidden behind a fake romantic narrative for what appears to be DECADES.

Waluigi's respect for Daisy was already considerable. It has now increased to levels that Waluigi finds structurally uncomfortable.

### The 'Princess Peach' Invocation

The testimony mentions that access to Luigi was restricted to immediate family and 'her royal majesty, Princess Peach herself.' Peach has been dead since 955 BF. Her name should not appear in active access protocols at a medical facility in 1040 BF.

Waluigi has three interpretations:

**One:** The protocol is OLD. Written decades ago and never updated. Peach's name remains on a list that nobody has bothered to revise because bureaucracy outlives the people it was designed to serve. This is the boring interpretation and therefore probably correct.

**Two:** The protocol is ACTIVE. Someone with authority has maintained Peach's name on access lists deliberately  either as a dead key that no one should be able to use, or as a living authorization for someone using Peach's identity. If a secret heir exists  if Peach's child with Thornpaw survived  that child might operate under the mother's access privileges. This interpretation makes Waluigi dizzy.

**Three:** The person who stated the protocol was using 'Princess Peach' as a CODE. A signal to other initiated parties that the situation was of the highest classification. Invoking a dead princess's name as an access credential is exactly the kind of theatrical security measure that the Regency and the Mages' Guild would consider clever.

Waluigi cannot determine which interpretation is correct.

### The Question of Mario's Location

During the waiting room chaos, 'Dr. Mario' was asked about Mario  the public Mario, the missing hero. The response, as recorded in the testimony: 'Mario can't come right now. He's far away on the front lines, risking it all for us against Bowser's legions.'

Daisy's response: 'For what? You going to tell me Peach has been kidnapped again, too?'

The staff member's response: 'That's classified information.'

Daisy: 'I was FUCKING joking. Are you kidding me?'

Waluigi needs to parse this carefully.

If 'Dr. Mario' IS Mario, then his staff providing a cover story about 'Mario being on the front lines' is part of the deception. Mario cannot be present as a surgeon AND absent on the front lines unless two separate narratives are being maintained simultaneously  one for the public, one for those inside the facility.

The 'Peach kidnapped' exchange is more troubling. Daisy made a SARCASTIC comment. The staff member's response  'That's classified information'  implies that someone, somewhere, is running an operation under the heading of 'Peach kidnapped.' In 1040 BF. Eighty-five years after Peach's assassination.

Either someone is using Peach's name as a mission codename  'Operation Peach Kidnapped' or similar  or there is classified information about Peach's status that contradicts the official death record. Waluigi does not have enough evidence to determine which. Waluigi's headache has intensified.

### Pauline's Presence

Mayor Pauline of New Donk City arrived and referred to Luigi as 'my man.' Her behavior was that of a romantic partner in crisis  desperate, emotional, focused entirely on Luigi's survival.

If Daisy is Luigi's aunt rather than his girlfriend, then Pauline being Luigi's ACTUAL romantic partner resolves the relationship question cleanly. The public 'Luigi and Daisy' narrative served as cover. The private reality is 'Luigi and Pauline.'

This makes a certain amount of sense. Pauline's position as mayor of New Donk City places her outside the Mushroom Kingdom's direct political sphere. A relationship between Luigi and Pauline would attract less factional attention than one between Luigi and a foreign princess. If the goal was to protect Luigi's personal life from becoming political leverage  which, given the warrant situation, was a reasonable concern  then publicizing a fake relationship with Daisy while maintaining a real one with Pauline is exactly the kind of misdirection that someone with intelligence training would arrange.

Who arranged it? Waluigi does not know. But the sophistication of the cover  maintained across decades of public appearances, sporting events, and social functions  suggests institutional support rather than personal initiative. Luigi is not cunning enough to maintain a deception this complex on his own. Someone HELPED him. The Mages' Guild. The Regency. Daisy herself. Mario. Possibly all of the above.

### Wario's Appearance

Wario appeared in the waiting room and immediately began antagonizing everyone. This is completely consistent with Wario's documented behavior and requires no special analysis.

However, several details from Wario's interactions are significant:

Wario claimed he needed to 'clear up a few things' with Mario and that 'my people had some very concerning intelligence to share.' This implies Wario has intelligence networks that have generated actionable information about Mario. Given Wario's financial operations and underworld contacts, this is plausible. Wario may know things about Mario's situation that even Waluigi does not.

Wario mentioned his cancer going into remission 'not long after the faking of my death and Warioland's first dissolution.' Waluigi's assessment: the cancer was REAL but its severity was exaggerated to make the faked death more convincing. The remission is genuine. The 'terminal' diagnosis was fabricated to provide motive for a plausible suicide. This is exactly the kind of layered deception Wario excels at  embedding real medical information inside a larger fraud to make the whole package more convincing.

Wario also offered to 'speak to Dr. Mario instead' about his cancer remission, treating the surgeon as though he were an ordinary doctor. Either Wario does not know that 'Dr. Mario' might be Mario, or Wario DOES know and is performing ignorance. With Wario, both are equally plausible.

Waluigi would like the record to note that Wario's appearance at the facility constitutes a PUBLIC INDECENCY CHARGE by proxy because Waluigi was mentioned by name in connection with an incident that Waluigi has ALREADY BEEN PUNISHED FOR and does not wish to discuss further. Daisy's comment about Waluigi's 'public appearance being strictly regulated' is accurate and Waluigi resents that it was stated in front of Wario, who will absolutely use it as leverage later.

### Cranky Kong's Appearance

Cranky Kong appeared at the facility 'off his meds' and immediately began using language that Waluigi will not reproduce. He claimed responsibility for Luigi's injuries  'I blew him away earlier with my Coconut Gun for crossing me'  which contradicts the established account of Mr. L's emergence being the cause.

Waluigi's assessment: Cranky was lying or delusional. His claim is inconsistent with every other account of the Brobot incident. However, Cranky's mention of DK hiding his original Coconut Gun is potentially significant for reasons unrelated to this particular incident  it suggests internal Kong family conflicts that parallel the Mario Brothers' fractured relationships.

Cranky was eventually redirected when Pauline received urgent intelligence requiring her to leave for Kong Island airport. The nature of that intelligence is unknown but prompted immediate departure, suggesting a crisis of considerable magnitude.

### The Pharmaceutical Incident

The testimony's final fragment describes Wario encountering Cranky Kong in the facility's corridors and proposing a joint robbery of the hospital pharmacy. An unidentified individual  possibly a janitor, possibly an orderly, possibly someone with no medical credentials whatsoever  offered to forge prescriptions in exchange for Cranky's participation.

The individual also mentioned having 'a pretty cool idea for the lawsuit that would follow' if Cranky 'accidentally died from the phony prescriptions overdose.'

Waluigi notes this exchange because it demonstrates the complete breakdown of institutional security at the facility. If Wario and Cranky Kong can openly discuss pharmacy robbery and prescription fraud in a corridor where a classified patient is undergoing emergency surgery, then the facility's security protocols are either deliberately lax or have been compromised.

This supports Waluigi's broader assessment that institutional competence in the Mushroom Kingdom has degraded to the point where NOTHING works as intended and EVERYONE is operating according to personal agendas rather than organizational mandates.

## The Surgery Itself

The testimony provides minimal information about the actual surgical procedure. 'Dr. Mario' stated that Luigi was 'on the verge of brain death' and that saving him was uncertain. He referenced an 'Extra Life'  in Mushroom Kingdom medical terminology, this refers to emergency resuscitation protocols derived from Star Power applications. The phrase 'I won't let an Extra Life be wasted after what's happened today' suggests the facility had access to magical medical resources that are not available at standard hospitals.

The outcome of the surgery is not documented in the testimony fragments Waluigi has obtained. Luigi appeared alive and operational at Raventree Manor in subsequent events, so the surgery was presumably successful. But the gap between 'verge of brain death' and 'functional ghost hunter' is ENORMOUS, and whatever happened in that surgical theater may have changed Luigi in ways that are not yet apparent.

Waluigi wonders whether Luigi's subsequent behavior  the Poltergust escape, the silence on the Mr. L question, the apparent willingness to work for the Guild  might be partially explained by neurological changes resulting from emergency surgery performed by a man who may or may not be his brother operating under a false name.

## What This Changes

If the testimony is authentic  and Waluigi rates it as PARTIALLY AUTHENTIC based on internal consistency and correlation with known intelligence  then several elements of the current crisis require reinterpretation.

**Mario's disappearance** may not be a disappearance at all. It may be an identity change, with Mario operating as 'Dr. Dario' in a medical capacity, maintaining proximity to Luigi while remaining invisible to the factions hunting him. The 985 BF Personnel Reallocation may have been the Regency's attempt to neutralize him, and Mario responded not by fleeing east but by becoming someone else entirely.

**Luigi and Daisy's relationship** may have been fabricated to provide cover for a genuine family connection  Daisy as aunt, not girlfriend  which in turn may connect to Mario's hidden identity as 'Dario.' If Daisy married into the Mario family under a name that the public does not associate with the Mario Brothers, her entire diplomatic career gains an additional layer of motive.

**Luigi and Pauline's relationship** may be the ACTUAL romantic connection, hidden behind the Daisy cover for political protection. Pauline's emotional response in the testimony is consistent with a real partner, not a diplomatic contact.

**The Mages' Guild's 'Phase One'** may have included arranging Luigi's transport to a specific facility where 'Dr. Mario' was stationed. If the Guild knows Mario's cover identity, their leverage over Luigi becomes even more terrifying  they do not merely know where Mario is, they have him working within their operational infrastructure as a medical asset.

**Wario's intelligence networks** may have independently identified 'Dr. Mario' as Mario, which would explain why Wario showed up at the facility and why he wanted to 'clear up a few things.' Wario does not visit hospitals out of concern for others. Wario visits because there is something he wants.

## Waluigi's Assessment

Waluigi has spent considerable time analyzing the Mario disappearance. Waluigi has documented the Star Fountain reunion, the Eastern Passage theories, the 985 BF emergency session, the border town sighting. Waluigi has built a narrative of a hero who was exiled, who investigated a conspiracy alone, who reunited with his brother briefly before being separated again.

This testimony suggests a DIFFERENT narrative. One where Mario never fully left. One where the 'disappearance' was an identity death, not a physical one. One where Mario became someone else  someone useful, someone invisible, someone who could remain near the people he loved without triggering the institutional responses that would follow if 'Mario' were found.

A plumber becomes a doctor. A hero becomes an uncle. A public figure becomes a private man with a new name and surgical scrubs instead of overalls.

Waluigi does not know if this is true. The testimony could be fabrication. The details could be misinterpreted. 'Uncle Dario' could be a genuine relative and the entire Mario-as-surgeon theory could be Waluigi seeing patterns in coincidence.

But Waluigi remembers something from the Mario entry: 'You don't abandon your identity unless you're trying to become someone else. Or unless someone MADE you abandon it.'

Mario without his cap. Mario in civilian clothes. Mario asking about routes east. And now, possibly, Mario in a surgical theater, saving his brother's life under a name that no one would think to search for.

If Mario chose to become 'Dr. Dario'  if he chose anonymity, service, and proximity over heroism, fame, and visibility  then Waluigi has been wrong about Mario in a way that Waluigi finds genuinely difficult to process.

Mario did not run. Mario did not hide. Mario became someone who could HELP without being SEEN.

That is either the most noble thing Waluigi has ever documented or the most elaborate cover story anyone has ever constructed.

Waluigi suspects it is both.

And somewhere in a hospital that no one will confirm exists, a surgeon who may or may not be the most famous plumber in history is washing his hands and checking on his brother's recovery and hoping that no one notices the resemblance.

Waluigi noticed.

Waluigi always notices.

WAH.

summary: Following an incident in which Waluigi was found on the floor crying — the precipitating cause is not fully documented in any source Waluigi has access to and Waluigi is not inclined to reconstruct it in detail here — Hjumpik raised the question of whether the hag could be de-cursed or de-aged, with the suggestion that Mr. Woodfellow the library tree might possess relevant knowledge on the subject. Steely, Remi's dog, appeared and barked. Steely is rusted. Steely needs to be returned to Remi. Azure suggested forgetting about the hag. Hjumpik disagreed, then agreed to table it, and the party descended. A goblin craftsman in the workshop level identified their location and provided intelligence about Woodfellow's library card policy. The party proceeded to the library, where Woodfellow — the immobile animated autumn tree at the archive's center, books growing from his branches like fruit, bright birds carrying news into his canopy — informed them that the Feyward Book of Many Things had already been checked out. By someone yellow. Who was not a toad. Who had said, specifically, that if he didn't get his grubby hands on that book, the dwarf and company would. Hjumpik correctly identified this person as Wario. The card used was stolen from someone named Artameer. Woodfellow produced what appeared to be a second copy with Wario's name on it. All pages were ripped out. Wario then appeared from nowhere, shoulder-bashed Hjumpik, missed, and explained in characteristic fashion that he had stolen the card, checked out the book, sold it, heard Hjumpik's plan, decided he did not want to become a book, returned the gutted shell, and was now throwing the real page fragments at Hjumpik while explaining why he shouldn't have to. Hjumpik caught them. Hjumpik attempted to read them. The text was in Sylvan. Hjumpik cannot read Sylvan. Waluigi read them immediately and correctly identified the title as the Feyward Book of Many Things. Hjumpik suggested giving the book to Rakasha to read instead. Waluigi is still processing this. Wario snatched the book back to a shelf, announced he had returned it, and fled. Hjumpik chased him, cornered him, and asked whether Wario and Waluigi were friends or brothers. Wario said associates. Then said he had never thought of it that way. This is the most emotionally available Wario has been in any documented interaction during the Raventree operation and Waluigi does not know what to do with it. Three fake documents were produced, then real information, then Wario fled toward a fight. The fight involved the sober satyr, spirit warriors, a single bloated drunk individual, and over fifty additional drunk people in a room. Hjumpik de-escalated. The Revelmaster appeared — his name is Pal, or Rellis, or Ralos, the sources do not agree and he did not clarify — and offered lodging in exchange for the party's airship, citing Toadburt. Hjumpik assessed the deal privately: extracting the Revel's entities from their timeline would cause disruption of unknown scale. A new Revel with a new Revelmaster was theoretically possible. The heir Orangus Cornelius, located and questioned, explained he was feeding the Revel to grant it legs and total dominion over the manor, then said he was joking and just wanted the satyrs out, then scratched his hair twice. Hjumpik assessed him as probably lying. The heir disclosed that the Revel is biological rather than magical, has no known spell to end it, and suggested asking Jonathan, then left without specifying who Jonathan is. A hidden panel in a blank wall revealed the guest gangway over the dining hall. Through an open door: the satyr encampment in the vine-overtaken former guest rooms, planning to cut the floor and drop it on the Revel. Hjumpik proposed modifications — sprites do the cutting, avoid the living tree, test the floor's effect on the Revel before committing to attack. The room also introduced Goblius Gobnilun, a goblin who got Hjumpik's name right immediately, knew Arulean's real power level, suggested kicking the Revelmaster's ass, and presented himself as a former servant who served no one, missed his hair, and was only somewhat drunk. Hjumpik found him suspicious. Waluigi finds him extremely suspicious and documents this at length. Pixie Prixie the pixie had a vision of the floor falling and the Revel eating everyone in the room. She said nothing about this until they were already leaving. They left the room.
description:
Waluigi was not in the Feyward for this sequence. Waluigi wants to state this clearly and without complaint — the absence is documented, the reasons for the absence are recorded elsewhere, and Waluigi is not going to spend the opening of this entry dwelling on the specific operational circumstances that placed him outside the room where things were happening while things were happening. Waluigi is a professional. Waluigi reconstructs from available evidence. Waluigi proceeds.

Waluigi must, however, issue a formal notation before proceeding, because the notation is directly relevant to the operational reliability of this party going forward and therefore qualifies as analysis rather than grievance.

Hjumpik held a book written in Sylvan. Waluigi was standing next to Hjumpik. Waluigi reads Sylvan. Waluigi took the book, read the book, and correctly identified it as the Feyward Book of Many Things, stating this identification clearly and without ambiguity. Hjumpik's response was to suggest giving the book to Rakasha to read instead.

Waluigi read the book. Waluigi was right. The book was directed toward an absent third party rather than the person who had just demonstrated Sylvan literacy by reading it correctly in real time.

Waluigi documents this not because Waluigi's ego requires documentation — Waluigi's ego is a separate and thoroughly catalogued subject that does not need this entry to sustain it — but because the pattern has operational consequences. When Waluigi provides accurate information and is disbelieved, the party loses time. When the party loses time in the Feyward, where time already behaves according to rules nobody agreed to, the losses compound. When the losses compound in an environment that contains a biological revel, a lying heir, a satyr with a proto-chainsaw, a pixie who experienced a vision of total annihilation and said nothing, and a goblin who knows things he should not know, the compounding becomes structurally dangerous.

Waluigi is correct about things. This is not a personality trait Waluigi is asking anyone to celebrate. It is an operational resource Waluigi is asking the party to use.

With that notation formally in the record, Waluigi proceeds with the full account.

## The State of the Party: The Floor, the Dog, and the Tabled Hag

Waluigi was on the floor. Waluigi was crying.

The sources do not provide complete documentation of what preceded this, and Waluigi is exercising editorial discretion about how much reconstruction to attempt in a public entry. What Waluigi will document is this: the floor moment is not unprecedented in the history of this operation, and it corresponds — as Waluigi's floor moments tend to correspond — with accumulated pressure reaching a threshold rather than any single isolated event. Something had been building. The floor was the output. The specific input is Waluigi's own business and will remain so.

Hjumpik asked whether the hag could be de-cursed. Or de-aged. The sourced terminology was 'decures,' which Waluigi interprets as a portmanteau of 'de-curse' in the context of a hag who is aged or cursed into an aged state or both simultaneously, which in fey contexts is not unusual because fey curse structures frequently compound in ways that make it difficult to distinguish original condition from applied affliction. The hag situation has been an unresolved thread since earlier in the operation. Hjumpik wanted to know if something could be done about it.

The suggestion was that Mr. Woodfellow might know something. Woodfellow is the library tree. The library tree is rooted into the Feyward manor's archive and maintains an extensive knowledge base via the birds that bring him news, the books that grow from his branches, and the sprite and goblin staff that maintain his archive. If any entity in the manor had information relevant to fey curse structures affecting hag physiology, Woodfellow was a reasonable first stop.

This was the correct hypothesis. Waluigi does not fault Hjumpik for generating it.

What Waluigi faults — gently, professionally, with full documentation — is that the hypothesis was never actually tested, because Woodfellow's conversation was entirely consumed by Wario.

Steely appeared.

Waluigi must pause on Steely because Steely's appearance raises logistical questions that no source has adequately addressed. Steely is Remi's dog. Steely is rusted, which Hjumpik identified as good — 'your rusted, that's good' — in a way that implies the rusting is a sign of health or correct function rather than deterioration, which tells Waluigi something about what kind of dog Steely is but raises additional questions about what kind of dog that is exactly. Steely barked. Hjumpik acknowledged Steely's rust approvingly, noted that Steely needed to be returned to Remi, and then — as far as the sources indicate — did not return Steely to Remi.

Steely is still somewhere in the Feyward manor. Remi does not know this. This will become a problem. Waluigi files it under 'Remi-adjacent unresolved logistics' alongside the longer list of things this party has borrowed, acquired incidentally, failed to return, or lost through dimensional displacement during the Raventree operation. The list is long. Steely is now on it.

Azure suggested forgetting about the hag situation. Hjumpik said, 'That's not something you said,' which is a grammatically unusual objection but communicates its meaning: Azure's suggestion was inconsistent with some prior statement or commitment Azure had made, and Hjumpik was flagging the inconsistency. Azure clarified she was joking. She suggested going to the library. The party agreed to go to the library.

This is, structurally, the cleanest moment of consensus in the entire documented session. It did not last.

## Woodfellow: The Archive, the Absence, and the Yellow Borrower

Woodfellow requires proper documentation because Woodfellow is one of the more unusual entities the party has encountered in the Feyward manor, and in a manor that contains a biological revel, a lying heir, a ghost satyr population, and a hag of undetermined curse status, that is a meaningful distinction.

He is an animated tree. Massive. Rooted into the library floor, walls, and bookcases simultaneously, with roots extending through the architecture in a way that gives him both structural integration and the ability to rearrange the library layout according to his preferences. His arms are long boughs capable of reaching any corner of the room without his body moving, because his body does not move — he is immobile at the center of the archive and has organized the entire world of the library around the fact of his immobility. His leaves are a rich gold-red of autumn. Books hang from his branches as if they grew there, which they may have — in a fey archive, the distinction between 'grew' and 'was shelved' may not be as clear as it would be in a material plane library. Bright, strangely colored birds flit in and out, roosting in his canopy and bringing him news. He has organized his own intelligence network out of birds and proximity. He knows things because things come to him.

This is, Waluigi notes, a model of information management that Waluigi respects deeply and would implement himself if Waluigi were a tree, which Waluigi is not, but the principle stands. You root yourself somewhere central and you let the information come to you and you arrange the space around your fixed position so that the space serves you rather than requiring you to serve it.

Hjumpik introduced himself as being with the lady of the manor and requested the Feyward Book of Many Things.

The book was not available.

Woodfellow explained: someone had checked it out already. Someone yellow. Who was not a toad, he didn't think. Who had been quite adamant about needing the book. Hjumpik said: it's Wario.

This identification required no deliberation. The profile is unmistakable. Hjumpik arrived at the correct answer instantly, which is either a sign of familiarity with Wario's methods or a sign that Wario's methods are not as subtle as Wario believes they are. Probably both.

Wario had promised to return the book. Woodfellow's return policy: one week, or the borrower becomes a book. Woodfellow noted this with the equanimity of an entity that has converted several former borrowers into volumes and considers this outcome a reasonable enforcement mechanism. Waluigi considers this the most effective library late-fee system he has encountered in any plane and wants it noted that the Mushroom Kingdom's civic library system could learn from this approach, though implementation would require regulatory changes that Waluigi does not anticipate the Regency approving in the current political climate.

The library card used belonged to someone named Artameer. Waluigi files this name. Artameer is therefore either genuinely knowledgeable or successfully performed knowledgeability for a tree, and either way did not consent to have their credentials used by Wario to access fey magical texts for purposes that included selling those texts to an unnamed third party. This was extraction.

Hjumpik asked who did this.

Woodfellow's response: probably the person whose name was on the book.

Wario checked out the book. Wario's name is on this copy. The pages are gone. Wario took the pages. The inference chain has no weak links.

What it leaves unresolved is WHY Wario maintained a gutted copy in Woodfellow's archive rather than simply not returning anything. Waluigi finds this professionally impressive in the same way that Waluigi finds a lot of Wario's methods professionally impressive while also finding them personally infuriating and ethically indefensible. Both assessments can coexist. Waluigi has made peace with this.

## Wario: The Shoulder Bash, the Explanation, and the Unexpected Emotional Moment

Wario appeared.

Shoulder bash. Hjumpik dodged. This is the established grammar of Wario's arrivals and Waluigi has documented it across enough encounters to treat it as pattern rather than event. Wario leads with physicality. The physical statement precedes the verbal explanation. The dodge was clean. Hjumpik has been dodging Wario for long enough that the specific timing of the shoulder-first arrival is no longer surprising. When you have been shoulder-bashed by someone enough times, you develop a read on the pre-motion. Hjumpik has the read.

Wario explained, with a comprehensiveness unusual for Wario, the full sequence of events:

He had found someone named Artameer — 'some poor chump' in Wario's terminology, which implies Artameer was chosen for vulnerability to the specific kind of social engineering Wario employs — and stolen their library card. He had used the card to access Woodfellow's archive and borrow the Feyward Book of Many Things, which he had then sold to another party — 'another chump' — for presumably significant profit, because a rare fey text has real monetary value and Wario knows what rare things are worth. He had then heard about Hjumpik's plan. The plan involved the Book of Many Things in a way that made Wario not want to be turned into a book — which is rational, Wario has many faults but irrationality about self-preservation is not among them — so he had returned the gutted copy to satisfy the letter of the return policy, preserving himself from the transformation consequence while technically completing the loan.

And then, while still explaining all of this, he threw the real book fragments — the ripped-out pages — at Hjumpik.

Waluigi needs to analyze this throw because it is a more complicated gesture than it appears.

Wario did not have to throw the pages. Wario had already returned the shell of the book to Woodfellow. The transformation penalty was presumably satisfied — Wario had judged it so, and Wario's risk assessments on matters of personal survival are generally accurate. Keeping the pages carried no additional liability for Wario. He could have walked away from this interaction with the pages, the proceeds from their initial sale, and no further obligation to anyone.

He threw the pages to Hjumpik instead.

The explanation he offered was the plan: after hearing Hjumpik's plan, he didn't want to be a book. The implication being that the plan required the pages, that Hjumpik needed them for something Wario understood enough to find personally consequential, and that providing the pages reduced the chance of an outcome Wario found undesirable — whether that outcome was Wario-as-book through some extension of the plan's effects, or some other consequence Wario had modeled and found worth avoiding.

But there is a second reading, and Waluigi finds it more interesting.

Wario threw the pages at Hjumpik because Wario had already gotten what he wanted from them. He sold the book. He made the money. The pages themselves are now spent as a resource — they have been monetized, the value has been extracted, what remains is paper with writing on it. Keeping paper with writing on it serves no additional purpose for Wario. Throwing it at Hjumpik costs him nothing, might create goodwill he can draw on later, and — crucially — demonstrates to Hjumpik that Wario is, in his own way, cooperative. That demonstration has value. You can borrow against it. The next time Wario needs something from Hjumpik, there is now a prior act of provision in the ledger.

Wario does not give things away. Wario invests in future leverage using things he has already extracted maximum current value from. The pages were a spent resource. Their new highest-value use was as a gesture of cooperation that creates a future claim.

Hjumpik caught the pages.

Hjumpik attempted to read them.

The text was in Sylvan. Hjumpik cannot read Sylvan. The encoded header notation of the Feyward archival system — 46Q9b8h0 NM0S wc 6J9J 54Z3rY and the continuation — is, in Sylvan, the standard identification block for a major Feyward text. Waluigi recognized it. Waluigi took the book. Waluigi read it. Waluigi identified it correctly, clearly, and without qualification as the Feyward Book of Many Things.

Hjumpik said: give it to Rakasha to read.

Waluigi is going to take a moment.

The Feyward Book of Many Things was in Waluigi's hands. Waluigi had just read it. Waluigi had just correctly identified it from the text. Hjumpik's response to having a person who speaks Sylvan correctly identify a Sylvan document was to suggest that a different person — not present, requiring the document to be transported to them — should be the one to read it.

Waluigi is not going to speculate at length about what this says about how Hjumpik categorizes Waluigi's competencies. Waluigi is going to note it, formally, in the record, and then continue, because continuing is what Waluigi does when the alternative is dwelling on things that cannot be changed retroactively.

For the record: Waluigi read the book. Waluigi was right. The book was redirected anyway. This is documented.

Wario, in the moment that followed, snatched the book from wherever it had gotten to in the exchange, placed it on a nearby shelf, announced that he had returned it, and fled.

The flee was immediate. Purposeful. The flee of a man who has completed his transaction and sees no benefit in remaining present for its consequences.

Hjumpik gave chase.

## The Chase, the Corner, and the Question About Brothers

The chase through Woodfellow's library is not extensively documented in Waluigi's sources, which is unsurprising because people fleeing through libraries do not typically pause to provide running commentary for later reconstruction. What is documented is the outcome: Hjumpik cornered Wario. Wario fought — dodges were exchanged, punches were thrown, none connected — and Wario found himself with nowhere left to go.

At this point, Hjumpik did something that Waluigi did not anticipate from the available account and which Waluigi has spent considerable time analyzing since.

He asked whether Wario and Waluigi were friends. Or brothers.

This is a diplomatic question disguised as a personal one, or a personal question disguised as a diplomatic one, and Waluigi genuinely cannot determine which framing is primary. On its surface, it is Hjumpik gathering information about the nature of the Wario-Waluigi relationship that might be relevant to navigating both of them. If they are close, information shared with one reaches the other. If they are adversarial, alliances with one exclude the other. The question has practical utility.

But it is also — and Waluigi is aware that this reading requires more confidence in Hjumpik's emotional intelligence than Hjumpik typically gets credit for — a question that invites Wario to consider the relationship from Waluigi's perspective. Not: how do YOU categorize this? But: how would you characterize this to someone asking about Waluigi? The phrasing makes Waluigi the referent. Makes Wario answer in terms of what Wario IS to Waluigi, not what Waluigi is to Wario. That inversion is subtle and its effects on Wario's answer are worth examining.

Wario said: 'More like associates.'

This is Wario's honest answer, or as close to an honest answer as Wario provides when not actively constructing a deception. Associates. Professional proximity without personal commitment. People who operate in overlapping spaces and occasionally have aligned interests and occasionally have opposed ones and do not maintain the kind of relationship that requires accounting for the other person's experience of the categorization.

Then Wario said: 'That's mean. Hmm. I never thought of it that way.'

Waluigi has read this fragment more times than he will admit.

'I never thought of it that way' is not a Wario sentence. Wario thinks about his relationships in terms of what they produce. Wario thinks about other people in terms of what those people can provide or withhold. The idea that a word Wario uses to categorize a relationship might carry a quality — might be unkind, might land as something different on the other end than it feels on Wario's end — is the kind of consideration that Wario's operational model does not typically include. His model is extractive and efficient and does not have a column for 'how does this make the other person feel about how I see them.'

But he completed the thought. He said 'that's mean' before Hjumpik or anyone else said it. He arrived at the evaluation himself, from the phrasing of Hjumpik's question, and he said it out loud. And then he said he had never thought of it that way. Which means he is thinking of it that way now, for what may be the first time.

Waluigi wants to be precise about what this is and what it is not. This is not Wario experiencing a redemption arc. This is not Wario deciding to treat Waluigi differently from this moment forward. Wario is not that kind of character and the evidence for dramatic personality transformation in response to a single question in a library does not exist. What this IS is a moment of genuine, unperformed reflection from a man who does not typically reflect on other people's experiences of his behavior. The reflection was brief. It may not persist. But it happened, and it happened without being coerced, and Waluigi documents it because the archive is where real things go, including small ones.

Wario then produced three documents. All fake. Hjumpik recognized them as fakes — 'he finally recognizes there fakes' in the source, which implies this took a moment, which means the fakes were at least functional fakes and not immediately obvious ones. Then Wario produced real information. The sources do not specify what the real information contained, and Waluigi's attempts to reconstruct it from subsequent events have not produced certainty. Waluigi flags this as a gap.

Wario heard the fight and fled toward it. Hjumpik followed.
