summary: After beating the original Dan nearly to death in the Corvinarus Sanctum's collapsing library — confiscating his spellbook, photograph, wand, water pouch, and the Bowser Badge numbered 447 that had been fused to his skin and triggered partial immolation when removed — Bowser looked up and found Orange T already there. Orange T had been present the entire time, treating Bones in the corner with the comfortable familiarity of someone who had established routines, watching the fight with the disengaged attention of a man who was either supremely confident in his own safety or completely indifferent to the outcome. He greeted Bowser with 'you put on quite a show,' deflected questions about his own presence with 'I'm here now and that's what matters,' suggested Bowser had a mission involving other Oracles that Bowser knew nothing about, pointed at something invisible and laughed when Bowser could not see it, identified Bones as being 'from the future' while simultaneously dismissing him as 'no one important,' and then — in what Waluigi considers the most consequential casual question of the entire sanctum sequence — asked whether Bowser cared what he did with the two unconscious Dans. Bowser, exhausted and not thinking, answered: 'Not particularly.' Both Dans were immediately banished. Bowser objected only when the Shadowfell Dan was already disappearing, producing the specific variety of regret available only to people who realize exactly what they should have said at the precise moment when saying it can no longer help. Orange T said 'oh oops.' Waluigi does not believe the oops. They continued into the clockwork observatory — a mesmerizing catastrophe of bronzed wheels, interlocking gears, and slow-motion structural collapse that produced sustained gongs of embodied dread with each impact. At a gap in the floor, Bowser offered to throw the Oracle because he loves throwing Toads and they are kind of dumb. The Oracle objected to the dumb characterization. Bowser dismissed him as Mr. Magic Man and then punched the observatory floor to demonstrate his power. The floor cracked — under BOWSER, not the Oracle, which early retellings got wrong and which Bowser has been correcting with pointed personal investment ever since. Bowser fell into the void. He caught himself on a floating blue seat. The Oracle attempted to move the seat with a tuning fork. Nothing happened. Bowser accused smart people generally of playing with his feelings. He then deployed a Lakitu lightning rod to harvest ambient electricity, climbed into a Goomba Shoe, and bounced through the dying observatory squeaking with every impact while recommending the footwear to the Oracle as a purchasing opportunity. They reached a telescope platform. The Oracle offered Bowser a look. Bowser looked and did not see stars. He saw the Mushroom Kingdom after Peach's assassination — his own past self refusing to accept her death, threatening to burn things, watching Thornpaw arrive and deliver the Mages' Guild deflection, growing increasingly violent until Luigi arrived with guards and fought him with misdirection lightning and the Poltergust in full combat deployment. Bowser watched Luigi defeat his past self. He watched Toad guards drag his unconscious body away while Thornpaw conferred with two hooded mages and the guards informed his limp form that it was not authorized to know what was happening. Bowser pulled away from the telescope, called the vision 'something sad,' and continued into the sanctum. Waluigi notes that this is the fourth major surfacing of Bowser's grief over Peach during the Raventree operation, the first time he was forced to witness it from outside his own perspective, and also not the most damaging thing that happened to him in the sanctum, because the Shadowfell Dan is still gone. WAH.
description:
Waluigi has assembled this account from Bowser's retelling, which required the standard deflation process plus additional careful excavation of the moments where Bowser's account went quiet — because what Bowser does NOT say is usually more revealing than what he does. The Oracle's perspective has not been independently obtained because the Oracle communicates in the register of someone who decided long ago that direct answers are a form of weakness. Orange T's contribution to this account amounts to 'I was there and I did some things' plus a series of deflections that Waluigi found professionally insulting. Waluigi has filled the gaps with analysis, inference, and the pattern recognition that comes from documenting this specific collection of catastrophe-generating individuals across multiple dimensional crises.

Waluigi must first issue a formal correction.

Early field reconstructions of the clockwork observatory sequence stated that the Oracle fell through the cracked floor when Bowser punched the ground. This is WRONG. BOWSER fell through the floor. Bowser punched the ground beneath his own feet, cracked his own footing, and dropped into the void below the observatory through a hole he substantially contributed to creating. The Oracle was standing approximately six feet away and did not fall. Bowser fell. Bowser caught himself on a floating blue seat. The Oracle then attempted to use a tuning fork to help, which is a different problem and will be documented separately.

Waluigi does not know why early retellings got this wrong. Waluigi suspects it is because 'Bowser punched a floor and fell through it' sounds like something that happens to Bowser, and 'Bowser punched a floor and the Oracle fell through it' sounds like something Bowser does TO someone, and the people relaying the story unconsciously upgraded Bowser's agency in the scene. Bowser himself has corrected this point in every retelling with unusual personal emphasis — not modesty, Bowser does not do modesty, but the specific insistence of someone for whom the EXACT sequence matters. It matters to Bowser that HE was the one who fell. Waluigi suspects this is because falling through your own punched floor is funnier and more honest than accidentally dropping someone else, and Bowser prefers honesty to a flattering revision even when honesty is embarrassing.

The correction is now in the record. Bowser fell. Everything else proceeds from there.

Waluigi also wants to state something clearly before proceeding with the narrative, because the narrative contains a moment that Waluigi considers the single most consequential careless statement Bowser has made since the Raventree operation began, and that is a competitive field:

Bowser lost the Shadowfell Dan through a two-word answer to a casual question. 'Not particularly.' That is the sentence. That is the cost. Two words, spoken without attention, addressed to a question about two unconscious men on the floor of a collapsing room, and the result is that a party member who Bowser physically carried through a grove, rescued from a Mazebound in a literal tug-of-war, and protected through a fight with a Mages' Guild operative — that person is now banished to an unknown location in an unknown plane with no healer, no allies, and no idea where he is.

Bowser's grief over Peach, his fight with Luigi, his complicated relationship with intelligence and manipulation — all of this matters. All of this will be documented in full. But Waluigi will not allow the emotional weight of the telescope vision to obscure the fact that the Shadowfell Dan was lost before Bowser ever reached the telescope, through inattention and the particular exhaustion of a man who has been fighting continuously since he fell through a midnight portal and does not have the remaining focus to be careful with his words.

The telescope hurt Bowser. What happened before the telescope may have hurt someone else worse.

Waluigi documents both.

## Orange T: The Toad Who Was Already There and Would Prefer Not to Explain Why

Bowser stood over the original Dan's body — beaten, cauterized, photographed, robbed of spellbook and wand and water pouch and the Bowser Badge that had been fused to his skin — and looked up.

Orange T was there.

Not arriving. Not entering. Already there, already treating Bones in the corner, already settled into the collapsing library with the comfortable familiarity of someone who had been in residence long enough to establish routines. Orange T occupied the Corvinarus Sanctum with the same energy that Green T had occupied the children's table at Orangus Cornelius's dinner — present in a space designed to make him irrelevant, positioned where powerful people would not think to look, and doing something more important than anyone watching would assume.

Waluigi does not know how long Orange T had been in the sanctum. Waluigi does not know how Orange T arrived. Waluigi does not know whether Orange T entered through the same midnight portal Bowser fell through, or through the planar connections the Oracle described — the sanctum's links to the Feyward, the Shadeward, and the ruined manor — or through some other method entirely. These are questions Orange T did not answer and Bowser did not press hard enough.

Bowser pointed. The gesture of a king who has decided that a finger is sufficient accusation without needing to specify the charge.

'YOU — what are you doing here?'

Orange T's response was delivered with the mild warmth of someone greeting an acquaintance at a party they were not especially excited about: 'You put on quite a show.'

He had been watching. The entire fight — the duel with the original Dan, the Scorching Ray backfire, the Fire Rune shackles, the acid elementals piercing Bowser's shell, the warhammer progression, the Bullet Bill cannon deployment, the final punch that sent Dan into the wall — Orange T had witnessed all of it without intervening, without assisting, without reacting in any way that Bowser noticed. He had been treating Bones in the corner and watching a Koopa king dismantle a Mages' Guild fire mage with the casual attention of someone observing a particularly vigorous sporting event.

People who watch violence without reaction are one of two things: supremely safe or supremely indifferent. Orange T's behavior suggests the former — that he was confident in his own protection, that whatever shielded him from the fight's consequences was sufficient that he did not need to move. This implies capability. This implies preparation. This implies that Orange T had reasons to be in this specific location that go beyond coincidence and extend into planning.

Waluigi does not trust coincidences in the Corvinarus Sanctum. The sanctum was BUILT. Intentionally. By people with enough power to construct a personal extradimensional reality and enough ego to fill it with marble statues of their own ancestors. Nothing in a built space is accidental. Orange T being here — already here, comfortably here — is not an accident.

'Shouldn't you be at the manor?' Bowser asked.

Orange T returned the question with mirror precision, the deflection so smooth it arrived before the original question had fully landed: 'Shouldn't YOU be at the manor?'

The exchange had the rhythm of two people establishing that neither is going to answer first, probing for which one will blink. Bowser is not a man who blinks. Orange T, it turns out, is also not a man who blinks. The standoff resolved not through concession but through Orange T simply choosing to end it — 'I'm here now and that's what matters' — which is not an answer but functions as one because it closes the door on the conversation while leaving the questioner no obvious way to reopen it without escalating.

'I'm here now and that's what matters.' Waluigi has heard this exact phrase, or close variants of it, from approximately one hundred people who have done something they would prefer not to explain and have calculated that asserting present reality is more defensible than providing historical context. It is a phrase that says: I have decided the audit of my reasons is over. You may accept this or you may not, but either way I am not continuing this particular conversation.

Waluigi finds this phrase deeply, personally offensive every time it is deployed. It is the verbal equivalent of someone drawing a curtain over evidence and then commenting on the quality of the curtain. The curtain is fine. Waluigi wants to know what is behind it.

Bowser accepted it anyway because Bowser was tired and bleeding and stranded in another dimension with more immediate problems than Orange T's origin story.

'I'd like to — oh yes — where are my fri— accomplices?'

Waluigi wants to mark that correction again because it is important every time it happens. The word Bowser started to say was 'friends.' He rerouted to 'accomplices' before completing the syllable. This has happened multiple times during the Raventree operation — Bowser initiating a word that implies emotional connection and substituting a word that implies professional arrangement before anyone else can hear him say something vulnerable.

The gap between 'fri—' and 'accomplices' is where Bowser keeps the things he is not ready to acknowledge. It is getting crowded in there. Waluigi is beginning to worry about the structural integrity of that gap under continued pressure.

Orange T pointed at something. 'Oh, them? They're in there.'

Bowser looked where Orange T pointed. 'Where? I don't see nothing.'

Orange T laughed.

Waluigi has spent considerable time analyzing this laugh. It is the laugh of someone who has pointed at something invisible and is watching a large, powerful person fail to see it — the quiet amusement of the knowledgeable at the expense of the uninformed. Whether what Orange T pointed at was genuinely there and genuinely invisible to Bowser due to some perceptual limitation, or whether Orange T was pointing at nothing and performing mystery for social purposes, is unresolvable from available evidence.

What Waluigi knows is that the laugh was not kind. It was not cruel either — not malicious laughter, not mockery in the cutting sense. It was the laugh of someone who finds a specific kind of entertainment in the disorientation of others. The Oracle laughs like this sometimes. The Oracle and Orange T share a register that Waluigi finds deeply suspicious, which may explain the Oracle's complete comfort with Orange T's presence in his sanctum and the Oracle's complete lack of concern about what Orange T is doing here.

Or perhaps they share the register because they are working together. Waluigi files this under 'hypotheses requiring evidence' and continues with the reluctant acknowledgment that evidence in this sanctum arrives on its own schedule.

## The Question About the Mission, and Bones From the Future

Orange T shifted before Bowser could press further on the location of the accomplices. He asked about Bowser's mission — specifically, the mission to kill the other Oracles.

This question landed with weight that Orange T either did not notice or chose not to acknowledge. There ARE other Oracles. The Oracle encountered at Raventree is not the only one. The nature of the Oracle — the 46-year-old interdimensional custodian in Toad years, the flesh vat collector, the person who warned Archie that he was absorbing too much power and then facilitated his departure anyway, the entity whose particular brand of helpfulness always seems calibrated to produce outcomes the Oracle finds acceptable rather than outcomes the party finds safe — implies a broader structure, a network, a system of which this Oracle is one node among several. If Orange T knows about other Oracles and knows about a mission to eliminate them, then Orange T has intelligence that goes well beyond 'manor-associated Toad treating a comatose patient in a room he will not explain how he entered.'

Bowser's confusion was genuine. 'Huh? What mission? I came barreling through and now I'm trying to find my accomplices. And I landed here — I thought we would reach where they are.'

This is the truth and Waluigi believes it. Bowser did not enter the sanctum with objectives. He entered through a midnight portal he fell into while chasing Markop's rescue, having already traversed the grove's Mazebound population, rescued the Shadowfell Dan from one entity in a tug-of-war, and beheaded another Mazebound in passing because ninety seconds of restraint was apparently his maximum. He fought the original Dan because the original Dan demanded a fight over which Dan had the right to exist. He is here because momentum and dimensional physics combined to deposit him here, not because he chose this location. Bowser's entire presence in the sanctum is accidental and consequential in equal measure, which is a ratio that describes much of Bowser's impact on the world.

The gap between what Orange T assumed — that Bowser arrived with purpose — and what Bowser intended — to find Markop and get out — suggests that information about Bowser's movements has reached Orange T through a channel that is not Bowser himself. Someone told Orange T that Bowser was coming. Someone described Bowser's presence in the sanctum as purposeful rather than accidental. Whether this is the Oracle, some observer in the Feyward or Shadeward, or the Corvinarus Sanctum's own surveillance mechanisms — and a sanctum with temporal telescopes almost certainly has surveillance mechanisms — is unclear. What is clear is that Orange T had advance notice and used it to form assumptions that do not match reality.

This is either intelligence failure on Orange T's part or deliberate misdirection — pretending to believe Bowser has a mission in order to see how he responds to the claim. Waluigi cannot determine which from available evidence.

'Well, one is here. From the future, at least.'

Bowser stared. 'Future? What do you mean?'

Orange T pointed at Bones.

Waluigi needs to pause here for the full weight of this statement. Bones — the comatose figure left in the Oracle's care by Archie Miser with the explicit instruction not to put him in a flesh vat, a figure whose identity has been a consistent mystery throughout the Raventree operation — is described by Orange T as being 'from the future.' In the Corvinarus Sanctum, where time dilation is confirmed and operational, where a month has passed in the Shadowfell since the planar fracture while only days have passed in the Material Plane, where the sanctum itself connects three planes whose temporal rates are not synchronized — the phrase 'from the future' is not a figure of speech. It is a navigational coordinate.

If Bones is from a future timeline relative to the current position, then Bones's identity may be connected to events that have not yet occurred from the party's experiential perspective. Bones might be a future version of someone they know. Bones might be evidence of an outcome that has already happened in one timeline but has not been reached in another. Bones might be a warning, or a weapon, or a variable the Oracle is managing with the same careful opacity he applies to everything else.

Archie said: do not put Bones in a flesh vat.

Orange T says: Bones is from the future.

The Oracle agreed to watch Bones and called it 'quite a burden.'

Waluigi is beginning to develop a theory about Bones that Waluigi is not ready to document because the theory is the kind of thing that, once written, cannot be unwritten, and because Waluigi is aware that he is working from fragmentary evidence in an environment specifically designed by people who understood observation well enough to build temporal telescopes into their personal reality. Waluigi will document the theory when the evidence is sufficient. For now: the phrase 'from the future' is in the record, attributed to Orange T, regarding the comatose patient the Oracle was explicitly instructed not to experiment on. Waluigi is watching this closely.

'Huh. Who's that?' Bowser asked.

'No one important,' Orange T said.

Waluigi has spent an entire career watching powerful people dismiss information. 'No one important' is the most practiced dismissal in the language. You do not practice dismissing things that are genuinely unimportant. You practice dismissing things that are VERY important when you do not want others to notice their importance. The smoothness of the delivery is the tell. You say 'oh, that's just the supply closet' with the ease of someone for whom the supply closet actually is a supply closet. You practice saying 'no one important' when the instinct to disclose has to be actively suppressed and replaced with a phrase that sounds like nothing, and you practice until the phrase sounds easy, and Orange T's phrase sounded easy in the specific way of something that has been said before. About Bones. To other people who asked.

Bowser did not press it. Bowser accepted the dismissal with the pragmatic acceptance of a man whose operational priorities are Markop, his accomplices, and getting out, and a sleeping stranger in the corner does not immediately impact any of those priorities.

Waluigi is pressing it. Waluigi is pressing it in the archive where pressing it is safe and where Orange T cannot deploy a smooth phrase to close the conversation.

Orange T walked up to Bowser with the confident proximity of someone who has assessed that Bowser is not currently dangerous to him specifically — a risk assessment that may be correct in the immediate tactical sense while being deeply wrong in any longer timeframe. 'Anyway — what do you need, tough guy?'

Bowser's response was theatrical: 'Hah! You will know the power of the Koopa King soon.'

Waluigi needs to document the full context of this moment. Bowser is covered in blood — his own from the acid elementals that pierced his shell during the Dan fight, Dan's from the systematic beating, and possibly some that belongs to neither of them and arrived during the Mazebound tug-of-war when he used the one-armed Dan as a rope and everyone involved got injured. He is standing in a collapsing room in a dimension he did not choose to enter. His accomplices are somewhere inaccessible. His healer is kidnapped into a cursed grove. His portal home is closed. His entire strategic position amounts to 'I am here and I have weapons.' And he tells a Toad of uncertain allegiance that the Toad will soon know the power of the Koopa King.

This is not bravado in the empty sense. Waluigi has documented Bowser's bravado across multiple incidents and has developed the ability to distinguish between its varieties. There is Bowser's combat bravado — functional, accurate, backed by genuine capability that Bowser has earned through decades of being the most physically imposing entity in most rooms he enters. There is Bowser's social bravado — the performance of confidence in rooms where confidence is a negotiating position, the particular volume of a king who understands that other kings respond to certainty even when certainty is partially performed. And there is Bowser's defensive bravado — the specific volume increase that happens when Bowser feels small and responds by becoming loud, which is different from the other two because it is reactive rather than chosen.

The 'you will know the power of the Koopa King' in this moment is defensive. Bowser felt what he always feels in rooms with knowledgeable, capable strangers who are not frightened of him: the particular vulnerability of being the largest, loudest thing in the room and still somehow feeling outmaneuvered. Orange T is not intimidated. The Oracle is not intimidated. The sanctum itself is not intimidated. And when nothing responds to Bowser's presence with the appropriate deference, he escalates the declaration. He cannot make the room smaller through volume. He tries anyway.

Bowser asked where he was. Orange T provided the architectural summary: a planar sanctum connecting the Feyward, the Shadeward, and the ruined manor. Three planes. One hub. Currently collapsing.

'Ha,' Bowser said. 'Looks like an asteroid hit this place.'

This is wrong about the cause and right about the result, and it is the most accurate inaccurate architectural assessment Bowser has delivered since he described the Raventree Manor library as looking 'like someone sneezed and the books decided to stay where they landed.' The asteroid theory contains no understanding of how extradimensional sanctums fail — they do not fail through impact, they fail through planar stress accumulation and temporal desynchronization and the progressive inability of constructed space to maintain coherence when the forces holding it together have been redirected or damaged. But 'looks like an asteroid hit this place' conveys the visual and structural reality with a precision that technical language sometimes fails to achieve. Waluigi respects this despite himself.

## The Banishment: Bowser's Careless Answer and Its Consequences

What happened next is the moment Waluigi has identified as the most consequential careless statement Bowser made during the entire sanctum sequence, which covers a substantial and competitive field.

Orange T, with the tone of someone asking whether you want the window seat or the aisle, looked at the two unconscious figures on the floor — the sleeping Shadowfell Dan and the critically wounded original Dan, both present in the library, both currently not a problem in the active sense because one was sleeping and one was barely breathing — and asked: 'Anyway — you care what I do with these two?'

Bowser said: 'Not particularly.'

Waluigi needs the reader to understand what 'not particularly' meant in Bowser's head versus what it meant to Orange T versus what its actual consequences were, because these three things are almost entirely disconnected from each other.

In Bowser's head: Bowser was tired. Not tired in the sense of needing sleep, though he probably needed that too, but tired in the sense of a man who has been in continuous crisis since falling through a portal and has been spending emotional resources faster than they regenerate. He had wrestled a Mazebound. He had carried the Shadowfell Dan through a grove. He had fought a Mages' Guild fire mage through escalating weapon deployment. He had been pierced by acid elementals. He was standing in a collapsing dimension with no allies, no healer, no exit, and an Orange T who was deflecting every question with the practiced ease of someone who has been deflecting questions professionally for years. The two Dans on the floor were, in this moment, problems he did not want to add to his processing load. The original Dan was a problem already solved through systematic beating. The Shadowfell Dan was asleep and therefore not immediately requiring management. 'Not particularly' meant: I have too many concerns right now to prioritize this. Handle it. I'll catch up. It was the verbal equivalent of waving at something while already looking at something else.

This is the mistake. Not malice. Not indifference to the Shadowfell Dan as a person — Bowser had just carried that person through a grove and fought a supernatural entity to retrieve him from its grip. The mistake is the exhausted imprecision of a man whose attention budget was already overdrawn, giving maximum permission through minimum engagement.

To Orange T: 'Not particularly' meant consent. Clear, explicit, uncaveated consent. Both. Take both. Do what you want with both. The king said not particularly, which means the king does not mind, which means the obstacle to disposal is removed and the spell can be cast. Whether Orange T genuinely interpreted the statement this broadly or used its breadth as cover for something he intended to do anyway is a question Waluigi has been sitting with since reconstructing this sequence.

A spell was cast. The kind of spell cast by someone who has cast it many times and finds the gesture economical — not dramatic, not effortful, the minimum expenditure of magical effort to accomplish the maximum result. Both Dans began to dematerialize. The original Dan — beaten, cauterized, Bowser Badge wound still seeping despite Bowser's attempt to close it with his own fire — vanished first. The Shadowfell Dan — one-armed, sleeping peacefully through his third consecutive dimensional crisis, completely unaware that a kingdom's worth of trouble had passed over him while he slept — began to follow.

Bowser saw it.

'HEY — wait — NOT THAT ONE. You're going to make a king mad!'

Too late.

The Shadowfell Dan was already going. The spell was already complete. The syllable of objection arrived after the sentence had been written and the ink was drying. Bowser reached the moment of protest at the exact instant protest became structurally irrelevant — which is the specific cruelty of regret in real time: you know exactly what you should have said, you can see with complete clarity the sentence that would have prevented the outcome, at the precise moment when saying it can no longer change anything. The clarity arrives with the door closing. The door was closed.

Orange T said: 'Oh — oops. I thought you said both were fine.'

Waluigi does not believe the oops.

Waluigi wants to be direct about this because Waluigi has been circling the question for several paragraphs and directness is overdue. A Toad operating within an extradimensional sanctum with sufficient magical capability to banish two unconscious people simultaneously — including a Mages' Guild fire mage who was specifically in critical condition from a badge-removal wound that had triggered partial immolation and been cauterized with Koopa fire, a man who would have required careful medical attention to survive transport — did not mishear 'not particularly' as 'yes, both, including the one I carried through a grove and rescued from a Mazebound at significant personal injury.' Orange T heard exactly what Bowser said. Orange T interpreted maximum permission from minimum specificity because that interpretation served purposes Orange T has not disclosed.

The question is: why did Orange T want the Shadowfell Dan gone? Waluigi has theories and none of them are comfortable. The Shadowfell Dan is a party asset — removing him weakens Bowser's position in the sanctum and removes a potential witness to whatever Orange T is managing in here. The Shadowfell Dan carries information about events in the Shadowfell from a firsthand perspective — a month has passed there, and the Shadowfell Dan has been present through some of that — and Orange T may not want that information reaching people Orange T is not certain about. The Shadowfell Dan is the one-armed version of the original Dan, whose relationship to the Liberated Toads, Green T, and the Mages' Guild is complicated enough that his existence represents a potential intelligence problem for multiple parties. Or — and Waluigi documents this as the most uncomfortable theory, the one Waluigi returns to at night — the Shadowfell Dan is relevant to Bones's situation in ways that require him to be elsewhere before something occurs.

Waluigi does not know where either Dan was banished to. The sanctum connects three planes. The Feyward, the Shadeward, and the ruined manor are all possibilities. Other destinations may exist within the sanctum's connective architecture — a space built by the Corvinarus family probably has exits and storage locations not visible on any available schematic. The Shadowfell Dan — who was present in the Shadowfell as a copy or alternative version of the original, whose origins are still not fully understood, who was in Bowser's implicit care — is now somewhere in a three-plane system with one arm, no resources, no allies, and the particular disadvantage of having been asleep when the banishment occurred and therefore having had no opportunity to orient himself to where he was going before he arrived there.

Bowser said: 'Ah, whatever.'

The 'whatever' is the sound of a man who has realized his mistake and decided that admitting the mistake — the full, explicit acknowledgment that two words of careless consent lost a person he had spent considerable effort protecting — requires more emotional exposure than he is prepared to perform in front of Orange T. 'Whatever' is Bowser's retaining wall. The verbal structure he builds between what he actually feels and what he allows to be observed. Behind the 'whatever': frustration at himself, concern about the Shadowfell Dan that he will not name as concern because naming it requires acknowledging it as caring and acknowledging caring requires acknowledging connection and acknowledging connection requires using the word 'friend' instead of 'accomplice,' and Bowser is not there yet, and may not get there, and is paying for the gap between where he is emotionally and where he lets himself be seen.

Bowser started to say something else. 'I want to get ouuut—' The word began to form, the complaint that was also a confession — I am trapped, I want to leave, this is not where I want to be, I fell through a portal and I cannot find the people I came here with and I just lost someone through two careless words and the room is falling apart around me — and Bowser caught himself before the sentence finished. He swallowed the last syllable. He sealed the retaining wall.

He does not want Orange T to know he feels trapped. He does not want the Oracle to know either. He does not want ANYONE to know, because kings do not confess to confinement, and Bowser is still performing king even when the performance is costing him things he cannot afford to spend.

They continued. Orange T leading. Bowser following. Into the collapsing observatory beyond.

## The Clockwork Observatory: Machinery, Dread, and the Floor That Bowser Fell Through

The passage between the library and the observatory was not a door in the conventional sense — in a sanctum that is progressively ceasing to maintain coherent architecture, the distinction between 'door' and 'wall that has given up' becomes increasingly philosophical. The space beyond resolved into one of the most disorienting environments Bowser has described in any retelling Waluigi has attempted to reconstruct, which is a high bar given that Bowser's retelling of the Shadowfell dinner party included the phrase 'and then I bit the bat' delivered with complete equanimity.

Bronzed wheels. Interlocking gears and sprockets in configurations that suggested a machine too large and too ambitious to ever have worked as intended, or possibly one that had worked perfectly and was now demonstrating what perfection looks like when it fails. Overhead, a massive wheel turned slowly, its spokes parallel to the floor — horizontal, not vertical, which is the orientation of a wheel that has forgotten what it is supposed to be turning and defaulted to the motion itself. Its circulation powered the rotation of numerous metal discs that glimmered in the undulating twilight and flashed with each burst of lightning that crackled through the collapsing structure's increasingly unstable ambient field.

At the diagonal corners of the room, wooden platforms extended beyond archway gaps in the stonework into the void of a starfield. Not windows. Not barriers. GAPS. The observatory floor simply ended at the archways and the platforms beyond were suspended over open void with the structural confidence of something built by people who either understood physics well enough to defy it or had not thought carefully about what happened if the suspension mechanisms degraded.

The machinery was dying. Not explosively — Waluigi notes this specifically because fast death and slow death are experientially different in ways that matter to anyone who has to exist inside them. Fast destruction is shocking and then it is over. Slow destruction is hypnotic in the way that irreversible processes always are — you watch things coming apart too gradually to stop and too inevitably to look away from. Gears wrenched from their moorings over the course of seconds rather than instants, colliding with each other in movements so slow that each impact had time to build anticipation before landing. Each collision emitted a cacophonous, sustained gong — not a sharp percussive sound but a RESONANT one, the kind that does not stop at the ears but continues into the chest cavity and settles there as a physical understanding of structural doom. Waluigi has heard this sound before. It is the sound of load-bearing elements discovering they can no longer bear loads. It is the sound that buildings make in the moment before they become rubble, slowed to a tempo that allows contemplation of the transition.

Bowser and Orange T reached a gap in the floor. A fallen gap — the absence of floor where floor used to be, opened by collapse into the starfield void below. Orange T jumped across with the practiced ease of someone who has been navigating this environment long enough to have memorized the gap's location and practiced the distance. This detail alone — knowing exactly where the gap is, jumping it without hesitation — tells Waluigi something about how long Orange T has been in this sanctum and how comfortable he has become with its disintegration.

Bowser offered the most characteristically Bowser solution: 'I can throw you if you want. I love throwing and bumping into Toads. They're kinda dumb.'

The Oracle, who had been somewhere in the observatory, responded to the Toad-dumbness assessment: 'I'm not dumb.'

'Yeah, yeah, Mr. Magic Man thinks he's not dumb.'

This exchange is Bowser's entire relationship with intelligence summarized in six seconds. Bowser categorizes by perceived capability, and the category for 'people who rely on magic rather than physical force' has been, throughout his documented history, associated with people who used their intelligence to manage, redirect, manipulate, or outflank him. The Oracle is unambiguously intelligent. Bowser's response to unambiguous intelligence he cannot personally verify or match is to dismiss it preemptively, which is a defensive move dressed up as contempt.

Bowser punched the ground.

Waluigi must be precise about the sequence here because the imprecision of earlier retellings is what produced the factual error this entry is correcting.

Bowser did not punch the ground near the Oracle. Bowser did not punch a section of floor that was structurally connected to where the Oracle was standing in a way that caused the Oracle's footing to fail. Bowser punched the ground BENEATH HIMSELF. He chose the section of floor he was standing on as his demonstration surface and drove his fist into it with the force of a man who has spent his entire life proving that physical reality responds to him even when people do not. 'See how powerful I am' — the words accompanying the action, the action being an assertion directed at the space and at the Oracle and at Orange T and at the general atmosphere of a dimension where nothing has responded to Bowser's presence with the appropriate level of deference.

The floor cracked. This is not surprising. The floor was already failing — the observatory was in progressive structural collapse, every surface compromised by the same forces pulling the gears from their moorings and producing the dread gongs. Bowser did not crack a stable floor. He accelerated the failure of a floor that was already dying, at the precise point where he was standing.

The crack network radiated outward from his fist. The floor gave way beneath him.

Bowser fell.

Not the Oracle. Bowser.

Bowser fell through the gap opened by his own demonstration, into the void of the starfield below, into the space between the observatory's collapsing platforms where the clockwork machinery's internal workings were presumably somewhere and the floating displaced furnishings of a sanctum that had stopped respecting gravity were also somewhere and Bowser had none of the navigational information needed to find a safe landing surface.

He caught himself. A floating blue seat — one of the sanctum's displaced objects, drifting through the void with the particular indifference of furniture that has stopped pretending it needs a floor — was in his path. He grabbed it. His fall arrested. He was now suspended over a starfield on a chair, having fallen through a hole he made in a floor he was standing on by punching it to show how powerful he was.

Waluigi pauses here to document the specific flavor of this moment. Bowser punched a floor to demonstrate strength. The floor demonstrated that Bowser's strength had consequences for Bowser specifically. The demonstration succeeded in the technical sense — the floor did respond to Bowser — while failing in the intended sense, which was to make the room understand that Bowser was a force to be reckoned with. The room understood that Bowser was a force. The force was then applied to Bowser. This is not the outcome Bowser was seeking but it is the outcome the laws of physics and structural engineering produced when asked to adjudicate the situation.

Early retellings incorrectly placed the Oracle at the center of this sequence. The Oracle was six feet away. The Oracle watched Bowser fall. Bowser has been correcting this in every retelling since with the particular insistence of someone for whom the exact choreography matters — and Waluigi understands why. Falling through your own punched floor is a specific kind of story. It is embarrassing, but it is YOUR embarrassment, earned by your own action, and there is a form of integrity in owning it rather than having it reassigned. Bowser owns his falls. He does not allow them to be credited to someone else's misfortune.

'I'm not used to this place,' Bowser said from the floating blue seat.

'What happened?' he asked, leaning — or hanging, or perching, depending on the exact geometry of the seat relative to the gap — with the belated concern of someone who has caused a problem and is now genuinely curious about its extent.

The Oracle produced a tuning fork.

Waluigi has spent more time thinking about this tuning fork than it probably deserves. This is a false statement. Waluigi has concluded that the amount of time this tuning fork deserves is actually quite large, because the tuning fork is the most concentrated version of Bowser's entire problem with intelligence in this sanctum.

The Oracle, positioned on solid ground above a Bowser who had just fallen through a floor he punched, produced a tuning fork and attempted to use it to move the floating blue seat — to resonate the seat into motion through acoustic or magical interaction, to propel Bowser back to solid ground through the application of a vibrating piece of metal to a problem that involved structural physics and dimensional void.

The tuning fork did nothing.

Nothing. The seat did not move. The void did not respond. The acoustics of a room filled with the sustained gongs of dying machinery are not a hospitable environment for delicate resonance-based manipulation, which is either information the Oracle did not have or information the Oracle had and decided to attempt anyway.

Bowser watched from the floating chair and tried to determine whether the Oracle was joking. The Oracle's expression — described by Bowser as 'like he was doing something reasonable and the world was being unreasonable about it' — did not resolve the question. Genuine use of a tuning fork as a propulsion device for a floating chair in dimensional void is either sincere incompetence or it is performance, and the Oracle is old enough in Toad years and strange enough in dimensional-custodian years that either option is genuinely plausible.

Bowser's conclusion emerged from a place that Waluigi recognizes immediately, because it is the place Bowser goes whenever he encounters intelligence that resists decoding:

'You're playing with me. Like all the smart people — they play with my feelings. I know, I know. Fine.'

Waluigi sets down his metaphorical notebook for a moment. Not literally — Waluigi always has the notebook — but the sentiment requires acknowledgment before the documentation continues.

Bowser has spent his entire life being outmaneuvered by people who consider themselves cleverer than he is. He was sent away from the Mushroom Kingdom when Peach was in danger — by someone smart enough to know that Bowser's removal was necessary and with sufficient authority to arrange it. He was told by Thornpaw that the Mages' Guild had it handled — by a man who knew exactly why Bowser should not stop looking and said those words anyway. He has been navigated, redirected, diplomatically managed, legally classified, administratively classified, and classified again in rooms where his physical capabilities were irrelevant to the conversation. He has been told he is not authorized to know things that directly concern him. He has watched smart people use the gap between his understanding and their information to produce outcomes he did not consent to.

When the Oracle produces a tuning fork and the tuning fork does nothing, Bowser's pattern recognition fires. This is what the smart people do. They make incompetent gestures that Bowser cannot evaluate and then something happens that Bowser did not anticipate and later understands was the real move all along. The confusion is the point. The apparent failure is the setup.

Bowser might be wrong here. The Oracle might genuinely have tried the tuning fork and it simply failed. But Bowser's wrongness, in this specific moment, is less interesting than Bowser's RECOGNITION of the pattern — the declaration that he has identified the shape of what intelligence does to him, the resigned 'I know, I know, fine' that acknowledges both the pattern and his inability to escape it even when he can name it.

Bowser has earned the pattern recognition. It comes from somewhere real. Waluigi does not know if the Oracle was playing with him. Waluigi knows that Bowser had reasons to wonder.

## The Lightning Rod: Bowser Solves a Problem Correctly While Still in a Floating Chair

Bowser did not sit with the frustration. He pivoted — which is one of Bowser's genuine tactical strengths that goes systematically underdocumented because his pivots tend to be loud and preceded by something that looked like incompetence, making the pivot itself look like recovery rather than strategy.

He produced the Lakitu lightning rod — the sleek, highly conductive metallic rod stolen from a hovering Lakitu's cloud. The tip crackled with latent atmospheric electricity. In standard combat deployment, Bowser uses it as a magical javelin: thrown, it draws static electricity from the environment during flight and strikes the target with a flash of white light that pierces armor and delivers a shock that leaves victims with hair standing at attention and a revised understanding of their own mortality. Bowser was not throwing it.

He held it upright from the floating chair. The sanctum's ambient electricity — generated by the progressive collapse of the observatory's machinery, by the planar stress fractures running through an architecture that was trying to connect three incompatible dimensional environments, by the interaction of forces the Corvinarus family apparently considered an acceptable operational condition — responded to the rod's conductivity with the efficiency of physics operating correctly in an environment where most other things were not. Lightning found the path of least resistance. The rod was the path of least resistance. The bolt struck the rod, channeled through the metal, ran its course, and Bowser stowed the rod before the discharge had fully dissipated.

Environmental energy harvesting. Not combat. Not demonstration — this time, notably, not demonstration, which suggests the falling-through-the-floor experience had briefly shifted Bowser's relationship with performing his power for an audience that was not responding appropriately. Practical interaction with the space's available resources, executed by a man who understood — perhaps not consciously in the analytical sense, perhaps through the accumulated pattern recognition of years spent fighting in magically active environments where ignoring ambient forces is how you get hit by them — that the electricity was there, the rod would attract it, and absorbing the discharge in a controlled way was preferable to letting it find its own path through whatever was nearby.

Waluigi documents this because it is the kind of thing that gets consistently lost in accounts of Bowser. The fireballs. The punching. The roaring. The bite on the vampire bat's wing. The tactical intelligence that operates beneath all of it — the environmental reading, the resource identification, the decision tree running faster than Bowser's verbal processing — this gets attributed to instinct and dismissed as if instinct were not a competency developed through decades of experience. It should be attributed to competence. Bowser in a field environment is not a blunt instrument. He is a blunt instrument shaped by long practice into something with considerably more precision than it appears to have.

He stored the rod. He took out the Goomba Shoe.

## Kuribo's Shoe: Bowser Navigates the Apocalypse Via Squeaking

Kuribo's Shoe. The Goomba Shoe. The massive, indestructible green boot with an internal wind-up mechanism that Waluigi has seen described in Koopa military procurement documentation as 'terrain navigation equipment for hostile environments' and in the field notes of soldiers who have seen it deployed as 'the ridiculous bouncing boot that somehow always works, we don't understand it either.'

Bowser climbed inside. A fully grown Koopa king — scales, shell, bulk, crown, and all the accumulated weight of someone who has been eating whatever was available in a vampire's dining hall and a hostile dimensional grove — folding himself into a boot designed for environments where the floor is made of spikes and hostile organisms rather than just absent. The Goomba Shoe's virtually indestructible sole treats spiked floors, Munchers, caltrops, and crumbling observatory platforms over starfield voids with equivalent disregard. Where there is floor, it bounces. Where there is not floor, it finds the next surface and uses that instead, because the shoe's mechanism was designed by Koopa engineers who decided that floor-independence was the relevant innovation.

Bowser bounced. SQUEAK. SQUEAK. SQUEAK. Through the collapsing machinery. Over the gaps. Past the gears separating from their moorings in the slow-motion funeral of the clockwork observatory. Across platforms whose structural integrity ranged from compromised to aspirational. The sustained gongs of dying machinery provided a backdrop of embodied dread against which the squeaking of an oversized boot provided something that was not quite counterpoint and not quite comedy but lived in the uncomfortable space between them.

'Be careful,' Bowser said while bouncing. 'You like my shoe? You should buy it.'

The Oracle, who had apparently returned to solid ground through means that Waluigi's sources do not specify, did not comment on the commercial opportunity. Orange T, navigating ahead, also did not comment. Bowser sold nothing. Bowser continued bouncing.

'You should put on shoes,' Bowser added, directed at the Oracle, which is practical advice offered by a man in an oversized boot who has just fallen through a floor he punched and concluded that better footwear is the applicable lesson. The Oracle's feet were, presumably, already shod in whatever interdimensional custodians wear. This did not stop Bowser from recommending the upgrade.

They walked — bounced, in Bowser's case — into the telescope room.

## The Telescope: What the Corvinarus Sanctum Chose to Show

The telescope platforms extended from the observatory's corners beyond the archway gaps into the starfield void. Each platform held a telescope fitted with a variety of lenses — more lenses than standard astronomical observation requires, the kind of array that suggests the instrument is designed to look at things other than stars, things that require different magnification, different focal adjustment, different fundamental assumptions about what constitutes a valid observational target.

The Oracle offered Bowser a look.

Waluigi considers this offer significant in ways that are not fully resolvable with current evidence. The Oracle did not have to offer. The Oracle could have proceeded. He chose, specifically, to draw Bowser's attention to the telescope and invite him to use it. The Oracle had just watched Bowser fall through a floor Bowser punched. The Oracle had no particular reason emerging from that sequence to do Bowser a favor. Either the Oracle was being genuinely generous — 'here is something worth seeing, you should have access to it' — or the Oracle wanted Bowser to see what the telescope showed for reasons the Oracle has not disclosed, and in the Oracle's documented history of behavior, undisclosed reasons for actions are the norm rather than the exception.

Waluigi does not know which interpretation is correct. Waluigi is going to document the outcome and let the reader form their own inference, which is an unusually humble position for Waluigi but feels appropriate for an instrument that shows observers what they most need to see.

Bowser looked.

The Corvinarus telescope did not show stars. This needs to be stated clearly because everything that follows depends on understanding what the telescope is. It is not an astronomical instrument. It is an observational instrument in the broader sense — a device for seeing things at distance, and in the Corvinarus Sanctum, the relevant distance is not spatial but temporal. The sanctum connects three planes. The telescope looks across time. Whether this was the Corvinarus family's design intention — building temporal observation into a planar hub for research, surveillance, or personal reasons — or an emergent property of instruments placed in a space where planar stress has been accumulating for years and temporal synchronization has been degrading since before Bowser fell through the portal, the result is the same: you look into the telescope and the telescope shows you something that is not currently happening.

The scene Bowser saw was the Mushroom Kingdom in the aftermath of Highsun 1, 955 BF. Not the ruined, fractured kingdom of 1040 BF. The kingdom that existed in the days following Princess Peach's assassination — the kingdom that was simultaneously trying to function and trying to determine what had just happened and trying to manage who found out what, in the specific way of political bodies that have just experienced a violent transition and have not yet decided whether to call it a tragedy or an opportunity.

Bowser saw himself.

Past Bowser. The Bowser of 955 BF — same scales, same crown, same fundamental architecture of a king who has decided something is wrong and is going to address it through presence and volume because presence and volume are the tools he has spent his life sharpening. Younger in ways that are difficult to quantify because Koopa aging is not linear and because grief ages people through mechanisms that do not show in scales or shell. This Bowser was standing in a Mushroom Kingdom corridor being blocked by two Toads.

'You can't pass,' the Toads said. 'She's dead.'

Bowser — past Bowser, telescope Bowser, the version of him that was THERE rather than watching — said: 'I KNOW she's alive! She's NOT dead! You want me to burn her?'

Waluigi needs to explain this sentence because it sounds insane and it is insane but it is insane in a specific way that reveals something important about what Bowser's grief does to Bowser's language.

'You want me to burn her' is not a threat directed at Peach. It is a threat directed at the world — at the situation, at the Toads, at the narrative being constructed around him in which Peach was dead and he was supposed to accept the construction and behave accordingly. Bowser's emotional vocabulary for unbearable situations has always been fire. When the world presents something he cannot fix, he offers to burn it — not because burning fixes the problem, but because burning is the only active response available when passivity is what the situation demands and passivity is what Bowser cannot do. Standing still in his own grief would have required accepting the information. Threatening to burn something kept him moving. Kept him in motion. Even if what he was doing was threatening to ignite a situation that was already ash.

He did not want to burn Peach. He wanted to refuse the world's claim about Peach by generating consequences for the world if the claim turned out to be true. The threat is not logic. It is the shape that love takes in Bowser when love has no functional outlet and the alternative is stillness.

Thornpaw arrived.

Waluigi has documented Thornpaw extensively. Chief Thornpaw of the Rakasha. Peach's secret lover. The man who knew about the hidden hatch behind the portrait — the passage through which he visited her privately, the same passage that the assassin used to bypass seventeen magical wards and four elite guards. Who was at Fawful's gala eighty-five years later and finally spoke about the relationship. Who exists in the investigation of the arrangement as either a key witness or, in the theory Waluigi least wants to be correct, something more complicated than a witness.

In the telescope, Thornpaw arrived at the scene where Bowser was being physically blocked from the chambers of a woman he had spent years circling in the particular way that Bowser expresses devotion — through repeated, dramatic, structurally questionable gestures that everyone interpreted as villainy but that were, at their core, a large fire-breathing creature trying to spend time with someone he found important — and told him: 'The Mages' Guild have it handled.'

Five words designed to stop someone from looking.

Thornpaw knew about the hatch. Thornpaw knew, therefore, that someone had used the hatch to access the Royal Suite without triggering the wards. Thornpaw knew things he did not say to Bowser in that corridor. And Thornpaw deflected Bowser toward the Mages' Guild — the same Guild whose operative Valorian Stormweave was at the Royal Vault that morning, knowing Lady Bloomia's name without introduction, delaying the crown delivery. The same Guild that assumed control of all magical evidence within days. The same Guild that has never released its findings from an investigation it completed decades ago.

Thornpaw told Bowser the Guild had it handled. And then Thornpaw backed away when Bowser's violence escalated, which was the tactically correct response from someone who had done the math on pushing past Bowser's threshold and decided the results would be unmanageable.

Then Luigi arrived.

## The Fight: A Tennis Match With Consequences

Luigi. Green cap. Green overalls. The Poltergust — the mechanical vacuum designed for spectral capture that Luigi has been using professionally to clear haunted spaces, including very recently at Raventree Manor where he also took a bubble bath and picked a lock with Iron Legion currency and obsessively checked the machine's integrity seals because it contained seven minor ghosts and two Red Zone entities he would not discuss. That Luigi. With guards running behind him, fanning out, establishing perimeter containment around the increasingly volatile grief-and-roaring situation in the corridor.

Luigi vowed to stop Bowser. To contain the situation before the King of the Koopas' refusal to accept reality produced structural consequences for the political arrangements very specific people were trying to make in the days following the assassination — days during which the Regency was consolidating, the investigation was being shaped, the evidence was being classified, and certain people needed certain other people to stop asking questions long enough for the managed version of events to calcify into historical fact.

Bowser saw Luigi and produced a broken tennis racket.

Waluigi cannot express how much this detail reveals, and Waluigi has been waiting for the opportunity to express it properly.

A BROKEN tennis racket. Broken before this fight began, at a previous point, at the match that Bowser immediately referenced: 'I remember you — the tennis match! Waluigi was there too!' Waluigi was there. Waluigi won his set. Waluigi is documenting this now because the documentation record is the appropriate place for this and Waluigi has been patient. But the tennis reference matters beyond the competitive score: Bowser had kept the broken racket. He had carried it from the match — across whatever distance and time separated the match from this corridor and this grief and these Toad guards — and it was in his shell-space or dimensional pocket, wherever Koopa royalty keeps things, waiting.

Waluigi knows why.

Throwing away the broken racket would have been accepting the loss. Keeping it is a refusal. Bowser keeps things he has not accepted losing: the racket, the letter to Peach written in elegant calligraphy forced on him by royal tutors with burn marks on the edges from the drafts he almost destroyed, the memory of every competition result he considers provisional. The losses are inventory. The inventory is evidence that the score is not final. He was standing in a corridor where Toads were telling him Peach was dead and refusing to accept it, and he had a broken tennis racket in his shell from the last time he refused to accept a loss, and perhaps there was some continuity there that Bowser felt even if he could not have articulated it.

He was also trying to find a version of Luigi that was not part of the apparatus trying to stop him. The tennis match Luigi was a competitor. A valid opponent in a clean contest with rules and a net and a score. THIS Luigi was arriving with guards to manage a grieving king into compliance with an investigation that the Mages' Guild was handling. One of these Luigis was someone Bowser knew how to respond to. He reached for the tennis match.

They fought without ceremony. Luigi jumped on Bowser immediately — the classic stomp, the foundational vocabulary of this relationship compressed into a single physical statement. Bowser absorbed it.

'You going to play this game, Luigi?'

'That's not over yet.'

Luigi clapped his hands. Green energy gathered at his palms. The visible buildup of a thunder strike — the preparation, the visual signal, the thing that Bowser recognized as a telegraph and prepared to receive. Bowser watched it. Bowser prepared.

Nothing happened.

Bowser laughed. The genuine laugh of someone watching something fail — relief and contempt combined, the specific satisfaction of watching the thing you were braced for not arrive.

Then the real strike landed.

Not the green gathering. The actual discharge — brilliant and white and fast enough that the sound was still arriving when the electricity was already through Bowser completely. It found him through the guard he had lowered in the moment of laughing. The gap created by relief was exactly the gap Luigi needed.

For one instant, Bowser's skeleton was visible through his scales. The current illuminated his bones from inside, the entire structural anatomy of a Koopa king made briefly transparent by the electrical throughput. Then the current passed and the flesh reasserted itself and Bowser was Bowser again, with smoke rising from places that should not be producing smoke and blood coming from somewhere and his mouth forming words before his voice had recovered enough to produce them.

'I didn't — you're a —'

The sentence had the shape of an accusation but would not organize into one. Luigi had hit him through his laugh. Luigi had known Bowser would laugh when the fake buildup produced nothing. Luigi had PLANNED for Bowser's laugh as a component of the attack sequence, which requires reading an opponent well enough to predict their emotional response and build that response into your tactical timing. This is not lucky improvisation. This is deliberate psychological strategy.

Bowser had been underestimating Luigi for the same reasons everyone underestimates Luigi: Mario. Being Mario's brother is an identity that arrives before you do and stays after you leave, and it positions you permanently as less impressive than someone else in every room you enter. Luigi had been doing something with the time not spent being impressive. He had been getting better. Getting strategic. Learning to build plans around other people's certainty that he was the lesser option, because that certainty creates exactly the kind of gap that a fake thunder buildup exploits.

Waluigi recognizes this approach with the recognition of someone who has employed it. The people told they are secondary either collapse into the assignment or they build something extraordinary in the space the assignment creates. They train in what is not expected of them. They develop capability in the register where no one is watching because no one thinks there is anything to watch.

Luigi had built something. Waluigi finds this both professionally admirable and deeply, privately concerning, because the same Luigi is currently working for the Mages' Guild and has gone silent on the question of whether Mr. L did something evil.

'Grr — I was going EASY on you!' Bowser said. Blood in his teeth. Smoke rising. 'THIS is how you treat me? You want to play the jumpy game? LET'S PLAY.'

He smiled. Coughing blood. The smile of someone who has decided that losing is not the narrative he is accepting regardless of the evidence supporting it as the only available narrative.

He invoked the Fire Rune. He activated Giant's Might. The ancient giant magic expanded him — scales darkening, eyes igniting with infernal light, the earth becoming aware of his weight in the specific way that ancient magic makes the physical world pay attention. The broken tennis racket in his hand became, in this expanded state, something between a sporting implement and a structural problem.

He connected.

Luigi was struck and driven backward into a bucket of flowers — an object whose presence in this corridor Waluigi cannot reconstruct and has decided to simply accept as one of those details that real events contain and fabricated events do not bother to include. Luigi was restrained in the flowers by fiery shackles, the magma chains of the Fire Rune holding him while they burned, the botanical context of the restraint adding a particular quality to the image.

'You like them apples, Mr. Thunder? How do you like them APPLES?'

Luigi struggled. The Fire Rune's Strength save requirement held. Luigi was burning and held.

Bowser breathed fire on the plants.

Waluigi needs to address this in full. Bowser breathed fire on the plants because fire is his first response to everything when he is in the elevated state that Giant's Might produces, and plants were the nearest flammable context, and the connection between 'plants are what is restraining Luigi' and 'burning plants will free Luigi' did not complete its journey through Bowser's processing before the fire was already in motion. This is the specific failure mode of Giant's Might combined with momentum: Bowser achieves a superior position, the superior position excites him, the excitement produces additional fire, the additional fire destroys the thing that created the superior position. This happens with some regularity.

The plants burned. The chains dissolved. Luigi was free. Bowser punched toward Luigi to compensate and hit a vase instead. The vase shattered. It was just a vase.

Luigi laughed.

The Poltergust activated. The blinding function. Then the electrical taser function. Then sustained illumination flooding the corridor. Three consecutive Poltergust applications that created an environment where Luigi had full positional clarity and Bowser had none. Bowser was heavily damaged, bleeding, huffing, spending the last of Giant's Might against a cascade of Poltergust effects he could not see clearly enough to counter.

'I'm not going out like this.'

The Bullet Bill cannon. The portable device he had carried through the grove and the portal and the original Dan fight without deploying — showing restraint across the entire sequence, using fists and fire runes and warhammer, the Bullet Bill cannon being the option kept in reserve for when everything else had run its course. Two Bills fired. They tracked Luigi with the mindless directional commitment of ordnance designed by engineers who believe every tactical problem has an explosive solution delivered at sufficient velocity.

Luigi was hit. He attacked. Bowser's counter missed. Luigi smirked. Then the Poltergust's capture function — full deployment, ghost-hunting power applied to a Koopa king, the machine that had contained Red Zone entities turned against someone who was not a ghost but who was, at this point in the fight, approximately as easy to contain as one.

Bowser went down.

Luigi was victorious.

Toad guards dragged Bowser's body across the corridor floor. As they dragged him, Thornpaw conferred with two hooded mages in voices too quiet to carry. The guards spoke to Bowser's unconscious form with the administrative dispassion of people executing protocol.

'You're not authorized to know about this.'

They told an unconscious king he was not authorized to know about the death of the woman he loved. They dragged him past Thornpaw and hooded Guild operatives having a conversation that required him to be unconscious and removed before it could take place. They classified his grief as unauthorized and his body as an administrative problem being relocated.

This is what cover-up sounds like from the inside. Not a dramatic conspiracy room. Not a villain's monologue. The banal machinery of institutional concealment: forms, procedures, authorized personnel, corridors that unauthorized bodies are dragged through, quiet conversations that happen after the inconvenient presence has been removed to a location where it cannot hear.

The telescope showed all of it. Every second.

---

Bowser pulled away from the eyepiece.

The observatory reasserted itself around him. The gongs of colliding machinery. The starfield through the archway gaps. The Oracle waiting with the patience of someone who has watched many people use this telescope and has stopped being surprised by either the duration or the silence that follows.

'Are you okay? You've been staring in there for a while.'

Bowser said: 'Yeah. I just saw something sad.'

Something sad. The word Bowser arrived at after sorting through whatever internal vocabulary was available and finding only the smallest possible container for the contents. Not devastating. Not life-defining. Not the thing that has been driving him for eighty-five years, the thing in the letter he carries, the thing that surfaces with Remi's 'Right...', with 'Is this a therapy session', with every moment the world reminds him that Peach is gone and he was not there and the people who made sure he was not there were never held to account for it.

Sad.

'Either way, let's go.'

They continued into the sanctum.

## Waluigi's Assessment: What the Telescope Cost, What the Banishment Cost, and Why Both Matter

Waluigi has documented Bowser's grief over Peach four times during the Raventree operation. Each instance adds something.

With Remi — 'Right...' — the grief was reflexive. Unconscious. Unguarded. Remi said she could not wait to meet Peach someday and the statement landed in Bowser's chest before he could deflect it and produced a single word and nothing more. He did not know how to explain it. He may not have known what it was.

With the question about moving on — 'Is this a therapy session?' — the grief was defensive. He recognized the territory and built a wall out of volume and misdirection because the answer is no and saying no out loud is a different kind of exposure than he is prepared for.

With the letter — 'Dear Peach, I heard you were here, I am NOT kidnapping you, unless you want to go? No wait, I am just visiting' — the grief is private. Not performed. Not defended against. Just present. The burn marks on the edges from drafts he almost destroyed and then kept because keeping matters more than quality. Bowser writes to Peach because stopping would require accepting there is no Peach to write to.

In the telescope, for the first time, Bowser watched his grief from outside it. He was the observer rather than the person experiencing the moment. He saw himself refusing the information. He saw himself threaten to burn something because burning was the only motion available when stillness was what the world demanded. He saw himself fight Luigi with a broken tennis racket from a match played before the world went wrong, because the racket was from a time when grief was not yet the context and carrying it into the hallway was a way of insisting the previous world still existed and could be returned to.

He saw himself lose.

He saw his body dragged across the floor by guards.

He saw Thornpaw talking to hooded mages while the guards told his unconscious form it was not authorized.

And he called it 'something sad' and kept moving, because that is the only thing Bowser knows how to do with things that hurt him.

Waluigi also documents the intelligence value separately from the emotional content, because both exist and both matter:

Thornpaw's presence and Guild deflection are consistent with the arrangement theory. He knew about the hatch. He directed Bowser away from the investigation and toward the institution controlling the investigation. His subsequent conference with hooded mages over Bowser's unconscious body is new data — not proof, but the kind of data point that fits a theory with aggravating precision.

Luigi's combat capability exceeds his documented profile. The misdirection thunder technique is designed strategy, not improvisation. The Poltergust's combat application sequence — strobe, taser, sustained illumination, capture function — is sophisticated multi-function deployment. The Luigi who takes bubble baths in haunted manors and picks locks with Iron Legion currency is also the Luigi who defeated a grief-empowered Koopa king through psychological misdirection and practiced tactical timing. Both are real. The gap between his public reputation and his actual capability is significant and getting larger as evidence accumulates.

Bowser's broken tennis racket as grief artifact: documented here because it belongs in the assessment and because it is the most human thing Bowser has done in the entire recorded history Waluigi has access to. He carried it from the match to the hallway. He used it in the fight he was conducting in the name of refusing to accept loss. The weapon he chose to fight with was the last object from the world that existed before everything went wrong. This is not strategy. It is the specific weight of things we carry when we cannot carry the actual thing we have lost.

But the assessment cannot conclude with the telescope. The telescope hurt Bowser deeply and produced intelligence of real value. The telescope is also not the worst thing that happened in the sanctum.

The Shadowfell Dan is missing.

The Shadowfell Dan was in Bowser's implicit care. Bowser had rescued him from a Mazebound in a literal physical tug-of-war, had carried him through a cursed grove, had protected him through a fight with a Mages' Guild operative. And then Bowser lost him through two words he spoke without attention to what they were consenting to.

The telescope showed Bowser being too late in 955 BF — arriving after the murder, unable to prevent it, dragged away before he could hear what was being said about what had happened.

In the Corvinarus Sanctum in 1040 BF, Bowser was too late again. Not because someone sent him away. Not because the conspiracy moved without him. Because he said 'not particularly' when he meant something more careful and Orange T used the imprecision as consent and the spell was cast before the objection could form.

Luigi hit Bowser through his laugh because Luigi knew Bowser would laugh when the fake thunder produced nothing.

Orange T banished the Shadowfell Dan because Orange T knew Bowser would say 'not particularly' when asked a question he was too tired to parse carefully.

Both were right. Both times, Bowser's predictability was the vector through which damage entered. The certainty that the fake thunder was the real thunder. The certainty that two unconscious people were not his current problem.

Bowser is learning things in this sanctum. He is learning them the way Bowser always learns things — through impact, through the quiet that follows impact, through standing in the echo of what just happened and deciding whether to call it a lesson or a failure. Usually it is both.

The Shadowfell Dan is somewhere in a three-plane system, alone, one-armed, with no idea where he is.

Bowser said 'let's go' and continued.

Waluigi continues to document.

WAH.
